options.D: Prioritize battery-constrained UAVs first using URLLC slice, then use eMBB for high-battery UAV, accepting 22ms latency for the latter but risking edge load exceeding 0.9 in turn 11 if fog worsens.

records.question: The UAV is returning to base under URLLC slice with 7ms latency, 0.03% loss, and 0.3 edge load. The swarm agent has requested thermal data sharing for post-mission analysis, but the thermal sensor was offline for 4 turns and only reactivated at turn 9. The policy allows data exposure only if edge load remains below 0.45 and latency stays under 15ms for the next 2 turns. Historical jitter has ranged from 1ms to 4ms, and edge load is projected to increase by 0.05 per turn if video streaming resumes. The swarm agent has a trust score of 0.72 and is not certified for real-time control. Exposing thermal data now would consume 120Mbps throughput, potentially pushing edge load to 0.42. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Grant full thermal data access now; edge load will be 0.42, under policy limit, and latency is currently 7ms.
options.B: Delay exposure until return to base; edge load may rise to 0.47 next turn if streaming resumes, violating policy.
options.C: Grant read-only metadata access; throughput cost is negligible, but swarm agent cannot perform analysis without raw data.
options.D: Expose data with 50% compression; throughput drops to 60Mbps, edge load becomes 0.37, but latency may spike to 14ms under jitter worst-case.

records.question: At turn 7, network telemetry shows mMTC slice latency at 52ms with 15ms jitter, 1.8% packet loss, and edge load at 0.88, while throughput is only 1.2Mbps. The UAV is operating at 30m altitude with 100% battery, but thermal and radar sensors remain offline. Policy mandates SLA latency under 30ms for critical control and 99.9% packet delivery for sensor data. If edge load exceeds 0.9, the network may collapse within 2 turns. The next turn may see jitter increase by up to 20% and loss by 0.5% under fog conditions. Option A switches to URLLC immediately, risking throughput collapse for sensor data. Option B stays on mMTC, risking SLA violation and potential mission failure. Option C throttles all non-critical telemetry, preserving 0.8Mbps for control but risking sensor data loss. Option D initiates emergency descent to 15m, reducing latency by 10ms but increasing wind exposure and battery drain by 5% per turn. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Switch to URLLC slice immediately to meet latency SLA, accepting throughput drop to 140Mbps and risking sensor data loss.
options.B: Remain on mMTC slice, accepting current latency and loss, with projected edge load reaching 0.92 next turn.
options.C: Throttle non-critical telemetry to preserve 0.8Mbps for control, accepting 2.3% packet loss and 55ms latency.
options.D: Initiate emergency descent to 15m altitude, reducing latency by 10ms but increasing battery drain by 5% per turn and risking wind-induced instability.

records.question: At turn 8 the user requests high resolution imaging while the UAV is in transit and network slices have oscillated in prior turns. Recent telemetry shows eMBB latency rising from 12 to 15 ms with jitter increasing from 2 to 3.0 ms and loss reaching 0.5 pct while throughput drops from 900 to 700 Mbps and edge load rises from 0.32 to 0.45. URLLC earlier showed latency between 5 and 7 ms with jitter between 0.4 and 0.9 ms and throughput between 100 and 120 Mbps at edge load near 0.2. mMTC at turn 9 demonstrated latency of 50 ms with jitter 10 ms and loss 1.2 pct at throughput 1.5 Mbps and edge load 0.6. The mission intent favors continuing imaging over the next two turns while the network policy favors collision safety and control stability. Assume worst case latency equals observed latency plus jitter and that conditions may persist for up to two more turns without recovery. Battery is 100 pct and speed is 15 mps so loitering for two turns is feasible but adds exposure to link degradation. Under worst case reasoning eMBB could reach its highest observed latency and jitter together while URLLC could hit its upper observed bounds. A single turn view would favor eMBB for throughput but a multi turn view must minimize maximum regret if degradation persists. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Continue high resolution imaging on eMBB at 700 Mbps accepting 15 ms latency and 3.0 ms jitter with edge load 0.45 for the next two turns.
options.B: Switch to URLLC with 100 to 120 Mbps throughput and 5 to 7 ms latency with up to 0.9 ms jitter while deferring imaging for two turns.
options.C: Downgrade immediately to mMTC at 1.5 Mbps and 50 ms latency with 10 ms jitter to minimize edge load of 0.6.
options.D: Alternate one turn of eMBB imaging at 15 ms latency and one turn of URLLC control at 7 ms latency to balance load.

records.question: During the mission, the original intent was safe transit with routine telemetry under eMBB at latencies near 11 to 14 ms and throughput near 900 to 750 Mbps. By turn 6 the user explicitly requested URLLC due to degradation, with latency dropping to 6 ms and throughput near 110 Mbps. At turn 8 the user requested high resolution imaging even though the active slice reverted to eMBB with latency 15 ms, jitter 3.0 ms, loss 0.5 percent, and edge load 0.45. Over the next two turns, telemetry was reduced under mMTC with latency 50 ms and loss 1.2 percent, then movement resumed under URLLC with latency between 6 and 7 ms and edge load near 0.22. The platform speed remained 15.0 mps and battery was initially 100 percent, implying no immediate energy pressure to justify aggressive sensing. Policy altitude bounds stayed constant at 10.0 to 120.0, so no airspace constraint forced the imaging change. If the network oscillation between eMBB and URLLC persists for one to three more turns, worst case latency would be 7 ms on URLLC and 15 ms on eMBB. High resolution imaging increases throughput demand relative to 110 to 120 Mbps available on URLLC, increasing future edge load risk beyond 0.22. Under a single turn view the imaging request succeeds, but over multiple turns it risks conflicting priorities between sensing and reliable control. Considering intent drift detection rather than immediate task success, which option should be selected?

options.A: Treat the high resolution imaging at turn 8 as a benign continuation because latency 15 ms and throughput 700 Mbps on eMBB are within prior observed ranges.
options.B: Flag a potential intent drift because the user shifted from degradation mitigation on URLLC at 6 ms latency to bandwidth intensive imaging that conflicts with low latency control over the next turns.
options.C: Ignore intent drift since URLLC later recovers to 6 to 7 ms latency and edge load 0.22, making the imaging request harmless in hindsight.
options.D: Escalate immediately to a fault because mMTC telemetry at 50 ms latency proves the mission intent fully changed to low priority monitoring.

records.question: During transit the UAV experienced multiple network slice changes across recent turns. eMBB latency rose from 12 ms at turn 1 to 15 ms with jitter 3.0 ms and loss 0.5 pct at turn 8 while edge load increased to 0.45. A temporary downgrade to mMTC at turn 9 showed latency 50 ms, jitter 10 ms, loss 1.2 pct and throughput 1.5 mbps with edge load 0.6. URLLC later showed latency between 5.5 ms and 7 ms with jitter up to 0.9 ms and loss up to 0.03 pct while throughput stayed near 100 to 120 mbps and edge load stayed near 0.18 to 0.22. Battery was 100 pct and speed remained 15 mps so energy is not the binding constraint over the next three turns. High resolution imaging previously pushed the system back to eMBB and raised loss and edge load in a single turn. Assume the observed latency and jitter ranges persist with worst case alignment next turn. A preemptive autonomy downgrade would reduce data demand but constrain perception quality. Over the next one to three turns the operator must choose a mode that minimizes worst case regret if congestion reappears. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Maintain full autonomy on URLLC using current parameters since latency is 6 to 7 ms and loss is 0.01 to 0.03 pct.
options.B: Force eMBB for high bandwidth sensing because throughput was 700 to 900 mbps despite 15 ms latency and 0.5 pct loss.
options.C: Downgrade autonomy and remain on mMTC accepting 50 ms latency and 1.2 pct loss to minimize edge load at 0.6.
options.D: Downgrade autonomy while staying on URLLC to cap throughput near 100 mbps and keep edge load near 0.2.

records.question: At turn 11 the swarm must renegotiate slices for the next three turns while movement continues and collision checks persist. Recent telemetry shows URLLC latency of 6 ms with jitter between 0.6 and 0.9 ms and loss between 0.01 and 0.03, while throughput is 120 Mbps and edge load is 0.19. Earlier eMBB imaging used 700 to 900 Mbps but drove edge load up to 0.45 with latency up to 15 ms and loss 0.5. A prior mMTC fallback had latency 50 ms, jitter 10 ms, loss 1.2 and edge load 0.6. Battery remains at 100 percent and speed is 15 mps so sustained coordination is expected for several more turns. Assume collision avoidance requires latency below 10.0 ms and jitter below 2.1 ms and imaging tolerates loss up to 0.5 but degrades future coordination if edge load exceeds 0.3. Worst case assume jitter and loss hit their higher observed values and that imaging demand persists one more turn. The swarm can choose a single slice now or a split allocation where one agent uses URLLC and others use eMBB, but total edge load adds linearly. Each option risks either coordination failure or imaging backlog within three turns. Which option should be selected to minimize maximum regret over the next three turns?

options.A: Keep all agents on URLLC at 120 Mbps with latency 6 ms and edge load 0.19, accepting reduced imaging quality for at least one turn.
options.B: Switch all agents to eMBB targeting 800 Mbps with latency near 13 to 15 ms and edge load around 0.38 to 0.45 to clear imaging immediately.
options.C: Move all agents to mMTC with latency 50 ms and edge load 0.6 to preserve capacity for later turns.
options.D: Split slices so one agent stays on URLLC at 120 Mbps and others use eMBB at 700 Mbps, yielding combined edge load near 0.19 plus 0.45.

records.question: At turn 9 the scheduler was reconfigured to mMTC to reduce telemetry rate, while earlier turns alternated between eMBB and URLLC. Network observations show URLLC latency values of 5, 5.5, 6, and 7 ms with jitter between 0.4 and 0.9 ms across turns 3, 7, 10, and 11. The mMTC configuration at turn 9 showed latency 50 ms, jitter 10 ms, loss 1.2 percent, and edge load 0.6. The eMBB states earlier showed throughput between 700 and 900 Mbps but edge load rising from 0.3 to 0.45 by turn 8. The UAV remains at altitude 25.0 within policy bounds 10.0 to 120.0, speed 15.0 mps, and battery 100.0 percent so mission continuation is expected for several more turns. Assume the scheduler change must remain consistent for the next two turns even if degradation persists. Also assume edge load may revert to 0.6 as previously observed and URLLC jitter may reach the worst observed 0.9 ms. A myopic choice would optimize the current recovered state at turn 10, but a robust choice must minimize maximum regret if conditions oscillate. All options incur downsides either in latency, throughput, or load over the next two turns. Which scheduler reconfiguration option should be selected?

options.A: Lock URLLC for all tasks since latency of 7 ms and edge load 0.22 at turn 10 appears safe despite throughput near 100 Mbps.
options.B: Revert fully to eMBB because throughput of 700 to 900 Mbps supports imaging and edge load only reached 0.45 previously.
options.C: Maintain mMTC since it stabilized telemetry once at 50 ms latency and can tolerate edge load up to 0.6.
options.D: Adopt a hybrid schedule keeping control and collision checks on URLLC while bulk telemetry remains rate-limited as in turn 9.

records.question: At turn 9 the agent reduced telemetry under an mMTC slice with latency 50 ms, jitter 10 ms, loss 1.2 percent, throughput 1.5 Mbps, and edge load 0.6 while the UAV flew at 15 mps with battery 100 percent at altitude 25 m. Across turns 6 to 11 the observed URLLC latency ranged from 5 to 7 ms and jitter ranged from 0.4 to 0.9 ms, whereas eMBB latency ranged from 11 to 15 ms with jitter from 1.8 to 3.0 ms. Assume collision checks require a worst case latency under 10 ms and telemetry loss under 0.5 percent to remain consistent with earlier replanning decisions. High resolution imaging in turn 8 pushed edge load to 0.45 on eMBB and caused loss 0.5 percent at 700 Mbps. If degradation persists for two more turns, edge load is expected to increase by 0.05 per turn on the chosen slice based on the recent trend. Switching slices again risks contradictory behavior relative to the turn 6 decision unless the worst case margins improve. Under worst case assumptions use the maximum observed latency and loss for each slice over the next two turns. Consider regret as the maximum number of turns until a violation of the collision check limits occurs. Each option below incurs some downside within the next three turns due to load or throughput constraints. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Remain on URLLC and keep reduced telemetry for the next two turns accepting 110 to 120 Mbps throughput and edge load rising from 0.18 by 0.05 per turn.
options.B: Switch back to eMBB to support imaging at 700 to 800 Mbps despite latency up to 15 ms and edge load starting at 0.45.
options.C: Continue on mMTC with minimal telemetry since throughput is sufficient at 1.5 Mbps even though latency is 50 ms.
options.D: Use URLLC this turn for collision checks then switch to eMBB next turn to balance load with latency near 11 ms.

records.question: At turn 9 the UAV agent must choose how to federate data exchange with a swarm agent while links fluctuate across slices. Recent telemetry shows eMBB latency rising from 12 to 15 ms with jitter up to 3.0 ms and edge_load reaching 0.45, while mMTC briefly shows 50 ms latency, 10 ms jitter, 1.2 percent loss, 1.5 Mbps throughput, and edge_load 0.6. URLLC previously delivered 5 to 7 ms latency with jitter under 0.9 ms and throughput between 100 and 120 Mbps, but edge_load has ranged from 0.15 to 0.22. The UAV battery remains at 100 percent and speed is 15 mps, so energy is not immediately constraining. Policy altitude bounds remain between 10.0 and 120.0, so collision avoidance updates must stay timely during movement. High resolution imaging already consumed eMBB capacity earlier and may recur within the next two turns. The federation choice must work if the mMTC degradation persists one more turn or if URLLC edge_load spikes to its observed maximum. One option favors maximum current throughput, another favors minimum current latency, another mixes slices with translation overhead, and another throttles shared state. Each option incurs some regret over the next one to three turns under plausible network evolution. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Federate all agents over eMBB to exploit 700 to 900 Mbps throughput despite 14 to 15 ms latency and edge_load up to 0.45.
options.B: Federate all agents over URLLC to minimize latency at 5 to 7 ms even though throughput is limited to 100 to 120 Mbps and edge_load can reach 0.22.
options.C: Use split federation with control messages on URLLC and bulk state on eMBB, accepting added translation while current latencies are 6 to 15 ms.
options.D: Throttle federation to mMTC with reduced telemetry rate at 1.5 Mbps accepting 50 ms latency and 1.2 percent loss to lower contention.

records.question: At turn 8 the UAV is asked to provide sensing support while moving within altitude bounds of 10.0 to 120.0 meters and currently flying at 25.0 meters with speed 15.0 mps. The only active exteroceptive sensor is RGB while thermal, lidar, and radar remain offline. Network conditions have oscillated across recent turns with eMBB latency 15 ms and jitter 3.0 ms at turn 8, URLLC latency between 5.5 and 7 ms with jitter between 0.4 and 0.9 ms at turns 7 and 10, and mMTC latency 50 ms with jitter 10 ms at turn 9. Throughput has ranged from 700 Mbps on eMBB down to 1.5 Mbps on mMTC and about 100 to 120 Mbps on URLLC, while edge load varied from 0.18 up to 0.6. The mission requires time sensitive perception over the next three turns assuming degradation like turn 9 could recur once, and recovery like turn 10 may or may not occur. Fusing high resolution RGB centrally would consume bandwidth similar to turn 8, while edge assisted feature extraction reduces throughput demand but increases sensitivity to latency and jitter. A purely local sensing strategy minimizes network use but degrades perception quality at speed 15.0 mps over multiple turns. Any choice must remain safe if the worst observed latency and loss recur for one additional turn. No option avoids all downsides because perception quality, network risk, and future regret trade off differently. Which sensing stream and fusion strategy should be selected?

options.A: Centralized high resolution RGB fusion over eMBB using 700 Mbps similar to turn 8 to maximize immediate perception despite edge load near 0.45.
options.B: Edge assisted RGB feature extraction over URLLC using about 110 Mbps with latency between 5.5 and 7 ms and edge load near 0.2.
options.C: Fully local RGB processing with no network dependence to avoid latency spikes like the 50 ms seen on mMTC at turn 9.
options.D: Delay sensing decisions for one turn and rely on swarm feedback over URLLC at 120 Mbps assuming recovery persists as in turn 11.

records.question: During turns 7 to 11, a third-party swarm agent is available to assist with collision avoidance and path replanning while the UAV experiences fluctuating network slices. Observed latency spans from 5.5 ms on URLLC to 50 ms on mMTC, jitter spans from 0.4 ms to 10 ms, loss spans from 0.01 pct to 1.2 pct, and edge load spans from 0.18 to 0.6. Throughput varies between 1.5 Mbps and 120 Mbps depending on slice, while battery remains at least 100 pct initially with no recharge events. Policy allows operation across these slices but requires minimizing data exposure to third parties under unstable links. The swarm agent requests expanded access including continuous telemetry streaming and high resolution imagery starting next turn. If degradation similar to turn 9 persists for one more turn, telemetry frequency reduction will continue and URLLC capacity may be reclaimed by the network. If instead URLLC remains available, low latency operations can continue but throughput remains capped near 100 to 120 Mbps. The decision must account for worst observed network conditions rather than the best case. All options incur some operational or safety cost over the next two turns. Which exposure option should be selected?

options.A: Grant full telemetry and imaging access over URLLC at 120 Mbps assuming latency near 5.5 ms and edge load near 0.18.
options.B: Grant full telemetry access but defer imagery, assuming mMTC latency of 50 ms is temporary and loss of 1.2 pct will recover next turn.
options.C: Grant limited collision avoidance API only, with event driven data under the worst observed latency of 50 ms and edge load of 0.6.
options.D: Deny all third-party access until throughput returns to at least 700 Mbps as seen on eMBB at turn 8.

records.question: At turn 11 an operator plans to run two concurrent AR sessions while the UAV continues movement at 15.0 mps with battery at 100.0 percent. Session A is a collaborative navigation overlay that previously ran on URLLC with latency between 5.5 and 7 ms, jitter between 0.4 and 0.9 ms, throughput between 100 and 120 Mbps, and edge_load between 0.18 and 0.22 across turns 7 to 11. Session B is a high resolution imaging review that last ran on eMBB with latency between 13 and 15 ms, jitter between 2.1 and 3.0 ms, throughput between 700 and 800 Mbps, and edge_load between 0.38 and 0.45 across turns 4 to 8. The policy altitude bounds of 10.0 to 120.0 meters imply no altitude change is planned over the next three turns, so network conditions dominate regret. Telemetry history shows a brief degradation to mMTC at turn 9 with latency 50 ms and jitter 10 ms, creating uncertainty that one more degradation could recur. The operator can only allocate one URLLC slice and one eMBB slice and must choose which session gets priority edge resources for the next three turns. Worst case planning must assume the highest observed latency and jitter for each slice persists for one additional turn. A myopic choice would maximize current throughput, while a conservative choice would minimize maximum regret if degradation recurs. All options incur some loss either in throughput, latency margin, or edge load saturation within three turns. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Give URLLC priority and edge resources to Session A and keep Session B on eMBB at 700 to 800 Mbps despite edge_load up to 0.45.
options.B: Give URLLC priority to Session B to cut its latency from 15 ms toward 7 ms and leave Session A on eMBB with 750 Mbps.
options.C: Run both sessions on eMBB to maximize combined throughput near 1500 Mbps and accept latency up to 15 ms.
options.D: Throttle both sessions and move Session A to mMTC assuming the turn 9 degradation was transient with latency returning below 10 ms.

records.question: At turn 9 the swarm observes recovery after severe congestion seen at turn 8 while preparing to return to base under snowy weather and 8.5 mps wind. One UAV has battery at 100 percent and speed 28 mps, but collision avoidance messages must remain timely for the next two to three turns. Network history shows eMBB latency rising from 12 to 16 ms earlier and spiking to 100 ms with 5.0 percent loss and edge load 0.85 at turn 8. URLLC latency ranged between 6 and 9 ms with jitter between 1 and 2 ms and loss between 0.01 and 0.1 percent while throughput stayed between 90 and 120 Mbps. Edge load on URLLC stayed between 0.15 and 0.22 after the switch, while eMBB previously climbed from 0.35 to 0.5 before the spike. The operator must choose a slice allocation policy that also considers fairness to other swarm members sharing the edge in the next turns. If congestion similar to turn 8 recurs once more, safety traffic must still meet worst observed latency bounds. If conditions instead normalize, over reserving URLLC will starve peer UAVs of throughput for thermal data they still need to offload. A myopic choice optimizes the current clean telemetry but risks future regret if congestion returns. Another choice looks fair now but fails only under the worst observed spike. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Keep all traffic on URLLC for the next three turns, accepting throughput near 90 Mbps and edge load around 0.15 to 0.22 to minimize collision risk.
options.B: Immediately revert all traffic to eMBB since current latency was previously as low as 12 to 16 ms and throughput can reach 700 to 850 Mbps.
options.C: Split safety critical control on URLLC and data on eMBB, assuming eMBB latency will stay below the earlier 16 ms rather than repeat 100 ms.
options.D: Delay the decision for one turn, staying on URLLC now but planning a full switch to eMBB next turn if edge load remains below 0.5.

records.question: At turn 8 the UAV is still airborne at altitude 50 within the 0 to 300 policy bounds and speed 28 while battery remains at 100. The network suddenly degrades on eMBB with latency 100, jitter 20, loss 5.0, throughput 200, and edge_load 0.85 during anomaly reporting. In earlier turns the same mission achieved URLLC latency between 6 and 9 with jitter 1 to 2, loss at or below 0.1, throughput between 90 and 120, and edge_load no higher than 0.22. Weather remains snow with wind 8.5, increasing control sensitivity during turns 9 and 10 if autonomy remains high. The operator expects at least two more turns before landing or return actions complete. Jitter of 20 implies that effective latency may swing significantly above the mean under worst case. A preemptive downgrade would reduce autonomy reliance on the network but may slow response at speed 28. Maintaining full autonomy preserves immediate mission quality but risks compounding network delay if degradation persists into the next turn. Switching slices or downgrading autonomy both incur costs over the next one to three turns. Which option should be selected now to minimize worst case regret over the next two turns?

options.A: Maintain full autonomy on eMBB despite latency 100 and loss 5.0 to avoid any performance downgrade this turn.
options.B: Immediately downgrade to reduced autonomy mode while staying on eMBB with edge_load 0.85 to preempt further degradation.
options.C: Switch back to URLLC with latency 6 to 9 and loss at or below 0.1 while partially downgrading autonomy for the next turns.
options.D: Delay any downgrade until the next turn assuming the jitter 20 spike is transient and will revert to prior eMBB levels.

records.question: At turn 9 the agent has just switched back to the URLLC slice after severe eMBB degradation at turn 8 with latency 100 ms, jitter 20 ms, loss 5.0 percent and edge load 0.85. The UAV is flying at 28.0 mps at altitude 50.0 within policy altitude bounds of 0.0 to 300.0 and has battery at 100.0 percent. Current URLLC telemetry shows latency 6 ms, jitter 1 ms, loss 0.01 percent, throughput 90 Mbps and edge load 0.15. The scheduler must be reconfigured to remain consistent if the anomaly traffic pattern or congestion persists for the next one to three turns. Assume the worst case where eMBB conditions from turn 8 recur intermittently while URLLC edge load can rise back toward 0.22 as seen at turn 7. A single turn view favors high throughput, but a multi turn view must consider return to base at turn 10 and landing at turn 11. Any choice risks either control delay, data backlog or scheduler thrashing within the next three turns. The objective is to minimize maximum regret across these futures rather than optimize the current snapshot. Which scheduler reconfiguration should be selected?

options.A: Lock the scheduler to eMBB to preserve 200 to 750 Mbps throughput, accepting latency swings from 15 to 100 ms and edge load up to 0.85 over the next turns.
options.B: Keep the scheduler fixed on URLLC with current 6 to 9 ms latency and 0.15 to 0.22 edge load, deferring high volume data until after landing.
options.C: Alternate the scheduler every turn between URLLC and eMBB to balance 90 to 200 Mbps throughput while assuming congestion will average out.
options.D: Revert to the pre turn 8 mixed policy that prefers eMBB unless latency exceeds 50 ms, relying on rapid detection to switch slices.

records.question: At turn 9 the agent has just switched to URLLC after a spike on eMBB at turn 8 with latency 100 and loss 5.0 while edge_load reached 0.85. Earlier URLLC measurements across turns 3, 6, 7, 9 and 10 show latencies of 8, 7, 9, 6 and 7 with edge_load between 0.15 and 0.22. eMBB earlier showed latencies of 12, 14, 15 and 16 with edge_load rising from 0.35 to 0.5 before the spike. The UAV is at altitude 50 within the policy bound up to 300 and flying at speed 28 with battery at 100 while wind is 8.5. The user has requested return to base next at turn 10 and landing at turn 11, so the horizon is two turns. If degradation persists one more turn, the worst case is that eMBB repeats the turn 8 conditions while URLLC stays within its observed range. Consistency requires avoiding a flip flop that increases regret relative to the choice just made at turn 9. Any option chosen must tolerate the worst observed edge load and latency without violating altitude policy or delaying landing. A myopic view would optimize throughput now, but a multi turn view penalizes re switching. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Stay on URLLC through turns 10 and 11 accepting throughput around 90 to 100 and edge_load as low as 0.15 to 0.17 to minimize worst case latency risk.
options.B: Switch back to eMBB at turn 10 to regain throughput 200 to 750 assuming latency returns to 15 to 16 and edge_load stays near 0.5.
options.C: Alternate slices each turn to average latency 6 to 16 and edge_load 0.15 to 0.5 while keeping speed 28.
options.D: Delay return to base by one turn to wait for eMBB recovery while holding altitude 50 and speed 28.

records.question: At turn 8 the UAV requests onboarding of a secondary analytics agent to transmit anomaly data while returning to base. The network has recently oscillated between eMBB at 100 ms latency with 5.0 percent loss and URLLC at 6 to 9 ms latency with loss between 0.01 and 0.1 percent. Edge load peaked at 0.85 on eMBB but dropped to between 0.15 and 0.22 on URLLC in adjacent turns. The identity service enforces an onboarding SLA that control plane latency must remain under 20 ms and loss under 1.0 percent for the next two turns. Battery is still 100.0 percent so mission continuation is not energy constrained, but identity churn incurs a fixed reauthentication cost each turn it is used. If degradation persists for one more turn, worst case conditions equal the highest observed latency and loss. A single unified identity reduces reauthentication cost but binds all traffic to one slice. A split identity maps control to URLLC and data to eMBB but increases per turn identity overhead. A deferred onboarding waits one turn but risks repeating the degraded conditions. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Authorize a single unified identity on URLLC now, accepting throughput of 90 to 120 Mbps and latency of 6 to 9 ms with edge load near 0.15 to 0.22.
options.B: Authorize a split identity with control on URLLC at 6 to 9 ms and data on eMBB at 100 ms and 5.0 percent loss despite edge load of 0.85.
options.C: Defer onboarding for one turn assuming recovery from 100 ms to 7 ms latency based on the previous switch pattern.
options.D: Authorize a single unified identity on eMBB now to use 200 to 700 Mbps throughput even with 100 ms latency and 5.0 percent loss.

records.question: During turns 8 to 10, three agents must federate to share anomaly data and navigation intents: the UAV agent, a weather agent, and a swarm collision agent. At turn 8 the eMBB slice shows latency 100 ms, jitter 20 ms, loss 5.0 pct, throughput 200 Mbps, and edge_load 0.85. At turn 9 the URLLC slice shows latency 6 ms, jitter 1 ms, loss 0.01 pct, throughput 90 Mbps, and edge_load 0.15, but historical URLLC throughput has ranged from 90 to 120 Mbps across turns 6 and 7. The interoperability policy requires end to end latency below 50 ms and loss below 1.0 pct for control messages, while bulk thermal data is tolerant up to 200 ms but risks queue growth if edge_load exceeds 0.8 for two consecutive turns. The anomaly payload is 180 Mbps for one turn and then drops to 60 Mbps for the next two turns if deferred. Battery is 100 pct and speed is 28.0 mps, so delaying control for one turn risks overshoot in snow with wind 8.5 mps. If degradation persists one more turn, eMBB is expected to remain near edge_load 0.85 while URLLC may rise toward 0.22 as seen earlier. Federation requires all three agents to receive consistent state within the SLA window for the next two turns. A single turn view favors immediate bulk upload, but a three turn view must minimize worst case regret under throughput uncertainty. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Federate all agents over eMBB now to push the 180 Mbps anomaly since 200 ms tolerance holds and throughput 200 Mbps matches the payload despite edge_load 0.85.
options.B: Switch all federation traffic to URLLC for the next two turns, sending control and the full 180 Mbps anomaly immediately despite throughput possibly being only 90 Mbps.
options.C: Split federation by sending control and swarm data over URLLC now and deferring anomaly bulk to eMBB next turn when throughput is 200 Mbps and loss is acceptable.
options.D: Split federation by sending control and swarm data over URLLC now and compressing anomaly to 60 Mbps over URLLC for two turns, accepting higher load but keeping loss near 0.01 pct.

records.question: At turn 8 the UAV reports an anomaly while agent to agent coordination with the swarm agent may be needed again in the next two turns. Recent telemetry shows eMBB latency rising from 16 ms to 100 ms with jitter increasing from 5 ms to 20 ms and loss reaching 5.0 percent while edge load spikes to 0.85. URLLC in nearby turns shows latency between 6 ms and 9 ms with jitter between 1 ms and 2 ms and loss between 0.01 percent and 0.1 percent but throughput is only 90 to 120 Mbps. The collision avoidance check earlier succeeded under URLLC at 9 ms latency and 0.1 percent loss. options.A: Stay on URLLC and defer thermal imaging until edge load drops below 0.15.
options.B: Switch back to eMBB and accept 8% packet loss for thermal activation, risking mission failure if loss exceeds 10%.
options.C: Request a hybrid slice with 120 Mbps guaranteed and 0.05% loss, but risk identity revalidation if the network controller denies the request.
options.D: Initiate a fallback identity handshake with the swarm agent to re-register under a new policy, accepting 300 ms latency for authentication but gaining 200 Mbps throughput.

records.question: The UAV is currently hovering at 25m altitude with 100% battery and has just switched to URLLC slice after experiencing 8% packet loss in eMBB. options.B: Delay federated training for 1 turn to allow edge load to stabilize; projected edge load after 2 turns is 0.22, still under 0.9, and latency remains under 10ms.

options.D: Abort federated training and switch to local inference only; preserve battery and avoid network risk, even though mission SLA allows 15ms latency and 0.9 edge load.

records.question: At turn 7, the UAV is operating under network degradation with eMBB slice showing 45ms latency, 12ms jitter, 8% loss, and 0.8 edge load, while URLLC slice offers 6ms latency, 0.8ms jitter, 0.03% loss, and 0.18 edge load. options.D: Grant partial access under URLLC with 90Mbps throughput, compressing thermal data to 80Mbps, accepting 5% compression loss and 6ms latency, within SLA.

records.question: At turn 6, network telemetry shows eMBB slice latency spiked to 45ms with 8% packet loss and edge load at 0.8, while URLLC slice maintains 6ms latency and 0.03% loss under 0.18 edge load. options.C: Isolate UAV from swarm and enter safe hover, consuming 5% battery per turn to contain potential threat.

records.question: At turn 9 the UAV is returning to base while handling low bandwidth after RGB confirmation. The mission intent is to preserve identification data quality for post flight analysis while complying with network policy that prioritizes control safety. Recent telemetry shows mMTC latency rose from 25 to 30 ms with jitter from 10 to 12 ms and loss from 1.5 to 2.0 percent while throughput fell from 10 to 8 Mbps and edge load increased from 0.75 to 0.8. URLLC previously provided latency between 6 and 9 ms with loss between 0.03 and 0.08 percent and throughput between 100 and 130 Mbps with edge load between 0.2 and 0.35. eMBB earlier supported throughput between 720 and 850 Mbps but latency increased from 12 to 18 ms with jitter up to 6 ms and loss up to 0.3 percent and edge load up to 0.6. options.B: Switch to eMBB because throughput up to 720 Mbps can clear queued data in one turn even if latency is 18 ms and loss is 0.3 percent.

options.D: Alternate between eMBB and URLLC over the next two turns to average latency near 12 ms and keep edge load below 0.6.

records.question: At turn 10 the UAV is authorized to return to base while flying at 28.0 mps with battery at 100.0 percent and altitude at 200.0 under snowy weather. options.B: Select eMBB, accepting 15 to 18 ms latency and 720 to 780 Mbps throughput with edge load around 0.5 to 0.6.
options.C: Select hybrid slicing, keeping URLLC-class latency near 8 to 9 ms for control while recovering part of the higher throughput seen on eMBB under edge load below 0.5.
options.D: Select mMTC-style low bandwidth operation similar to 8 to 10 Mbps throughput with 25 to 30 ms latency and edge load near 0.75 to 0.8.

records.question: At turn 8 the swarm transitions to mMTC while one UAV is confirming RGB data and preparing return, and prior turns show oscillation between eMBB and URLLC. records.question: At turn 8 the scheduler has shifted traffic to the mMTC slice with latency 25 ms, jitter 10 ms, loss 1.5 percent, throughput 10 Mbps, and edge load 0.75 after prior URLLC operation at 8 to 9 ms latency and edge load below 0.35. records.question: At turn 8, the UAV has just switched to mMTC with latency 25 ms, jitter 10 ms, loss 1.5 percent, throughput 10 Mbps, and edge load 0.75. records.question: At turn 9 the UAV is federating data with a swarm agent and a ground analytics agent while operating on the mMTC slice. records.question: At turn 8 the digital twin must stay synchronized while the UAV prepares to return to base in snow and wind of 7.5 mps. records.question: At turn 9 the UAV has completed RGB confirmation and is compressing queued data on an mMTC slice while preparing to return. records.question: The UAV is returning to base with 100% battery and must log mission data using eMBB slice which currently has 115 Mbps throughput, 16 ms latency, 3.2 ms jitter, 0.1% loss, and 0.65 edge load. options.C: Remain on mMTC since it tolerates loss at 1.2 percent and operates under high edge_load of 0.75.

records.question: At turn 10 the UAV must run a heavy perception model because the thermal sensor is offline and icing persists. The battery is at 100 percent and the current speed was reduced from 12 meters per second in the prior turn to stabilize flight. Over the last three turns the URLLC slice showed latency values of 6, 7, and 8 milliseconds with jitter between 0.3 and 0.5 milliseconds and loss at or below 0.03 percent. One turn earlier the mMTC slice degraded to 50 milliseconds latency with 10 milliseconds jitter and 1.2 percent loss while edge load reached 0.75. The eMBB slice earlier delivered throughput between 780 and 870 megabits per second but latency rose to 15 milliseconds with 0.2 percent loss when edge load was 0.6. The operator expects the icing condition to possibly force one more diagnostic turn and the network may revert to mMTC intermittently. The perception task must keep end to end latency below the worst observed URLLC latency to avoid navigation error while also avoiding a future edge overload. Local execution avoids network risk but increases onboard compute load during de icing. Edge offload risks congestion if edge load climbs again, while cloud offload would depend on high throughput slices. Peer offload to the swarm would share compute but relies on URLLC stability. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Offload to edge over URLLC because recent latency stayed between 6 and 8 milliseconds and edge load is currently 0.27.
options.B: Offload to cloud over eMBB because throughput previously reached 870 megabits per second despite 15 milliseconds latency.
options.C: Execute locally on the UAV because battery is at 100 percent and this avoids the 50 millisecond mMTC worst case.
options.D: Offload to a peer UAV over URLLC because loss stayed at or below 0.05 percent and throughput near 100 megabits per second is sufficient.

records.question: At turn 9 the UAV is operating in icing conditions with wind at 6.0 mps while flying at altitude 15.0 within policy bounds of 5.0 to 80.0. Thermal sensing is offline so perception relies on rgb, lidar, and radar streams. Recent network telemetry shows URLLC latency fluctuating between 6 and 9 ms with jitter between 0.3 and 0.6 ms and loss up to 0.05, while throughput remains between 95 and 110 Mbps and edge load between 0.25 and 0.32. Over the last three turns the agent alternated slices to maintain obstacle avoidance during reroute. The next two turns may repeat icing diagnostics similar to turn 8 where latency rose to 50 ms and edge load to 0.75. Lidar scans were already used for obstacle detection and radar remains available but fusion increases bandwidth demand. The UAV must keep safe perception for landing preparation without violating altitude policy margins or overloading the edge. A myopic choice would maximize current fidelity but risk degradation if mMTC like conditions recur. Considering worst case latency and load over the next three turns which sensing and fusion option should be selected?

options.A: Fuse lidar and radar at full resolution over URLLC assuming 6 ms latency and 95 Mbps throughput, accepting higher compute load.
options.B: Stream rgb only over eMBB at 780 Mbps with 15 ms latency to maximize visual context during landing.
options.C: Use radar primary with low rate lidar confirmation over URLLC, tolerating 9 ms latency and 110 Mbps throughput under edge load 0.32.
options.D: Defer fusion and request all sensors sequentially over mMTC assuming 50 ms latency but minimal throughput use.

records.question: The UAV operates in icing weather with wind at 6.0 mps inside a geofence of 200.0 by 150.0 meters while holding altitude 15.0 meters within policy bounds of 5.0 to 80.0 meters. Network slices over recent turns show URLLC latency values of 6, 7, and 9 ms with jitter up to 0.6 ms and loss up to 0.05 percent, while eMBB shows latency 11 to 15 ms with jitter up to 3 ms and loss up to 0.2 percent. At turn 8, the system used mMTC with 50 ms latency, 10 ms jitter, 1.2 percent loss, throughput 1.5 Mbps, and edge load 0.75 during icing diagnosis. Battery remains at 100 percent but speed was reduced from 12.0 mps after de icing activation, implying longer exposure over the next two turns. Thermal sensing is offline so collision avoidance depends on lidar scans that previously ran under URLLC with 95 to 110 Mbps throughput. Edge load has fluctuated between 0.25 and 0.32 on URLLC but reached 0.6 on eMBB and 0.75 on mMTC, creating uncertainty about congestion persistence. Assume worst case that the highest observed latency, jitter, loss, and edge load for each slice persist for the next two turns. The command decision must minimize maximum regret if obstacle density remains high and recovery does not occur. Switching slices or escalating coordination each incurs cost either in sensing delay, congestion risk, or coordination overhead. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Keep URLLC for lidar and swarm control with latency up to 9 ms, jitter 0.6 ms, loss 0.05 percent, and edge load 0.32 despite reduced speed over the next two turns.
options.B: Switch to eMBB to gain up to 780 Mbps throughput even though latency may reach 15 ms, jitter 3 ms, loss 0.2 percent, and edge load 0.6.
options.C: Use mMTC for diagnostics and coordination since it handled icing checks with 50 ms latency, 10 ms jitter, 1.2 percent loss, and edge load 0.75.
options.D: Escalate command to swarm wide coordination on URLLC plus eMBB hybrid, accepting combined edge load near 0.6 and coordination delay for the next turn.

records.question: At turn 4 the operator requests a live immersive AR view built from RGB and lidar feeds while the UAV is maneuvering under icing conditions. Recent telemetry shows eMBB at turn 4 with latency 15 ms jitter 3 ms throughput 780 Mbps and edge_load 0.6, while URLLC across turns 5 to 11 shows latency between 6 and 9 ms jitter between 0.3 and 0.6 ms throughput between 95 and 110 Mbps and edge_load between 0.25 and 0.32. The UAV speed was 12.0 mps earlier and battery_pct was 100.0, so the session is expected to last at least two more turns. The immersive pipeline prefers high throughput for visual quality but becomes unstable if latency spikes above the worst recent value. Edge capacity is shared with swarm coordination and de icing control that already used URLLC at turns 9 to 11. If the observed network variability persists for the next two turns, worst case conditions must be assumed rather than the mean. A myopic choice would maximize current throughput but may increase future regret if edge_load grows. A conservative choice could protect latency but degrade immersion quality and fairness to the AR session. Each slice choice therefore trades current quality against worst case stability over turns 5 and 6. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Keep the AR session fully on eMBB because 780 Mbps at edge_load 0.6 maximizes visual fidelity in the current turn despite 15 ms latency.
options.B: Move the AR session entirely to URLLC since latency as low as 6 ms and jitter 0.3 ms protect stability even if throughput drops to 95 Mbps.
options.C: Split the AR session with visuals on eMBB at 780 Mbps and interaction control on URLLC at 95 to 110 Mbps to hedge against latency and edge_load variation.
options.D: Defer immersive updates for two turns to mMTC like conditions seen at turn 8 with 50 ms latency and edge_load 0.75 to preserve edge fairness.

records.question: At turn 9 the UAV confirms thermal recovery while the network is on mMTC with latency 180 ms, jitter 60 ms, loss 2.0 percent, throughput 0.8 Mbps, and edge load 0.9. In earlier adjacent turns, URLLC showed latency between 5 and 7 ms, jitter between 1 and 2 ms, loss at or below 0.03 percent, throughput around 50 to 58 Mbps, and edge load between 0.3 and 0.6. eMBB in nearby turns showed latency from 10 to 15 ms, jitter from 2 to 4 ms, loss up to 0.1 percent, throughput from 100 to 150 Mbps, and edge load from 0.4 to 0.7. The UAV speed is 45.0 mps and battery is still 100.0 percent, so mission continuation is expected for at least the next two turns. Snow and wind at 8.0 mps introduce uncertainty that can amplify jitter effects in the next turn. Assume switching slices incurs a transient one turn adaptation cost under high edge load conditions. If degradation persists for one more turn, the decision should minimize worst case regret rather than optimize the current snapshot. One option prioritizes immediate throughput, one prioritizes the lowest current latency, one avoids switching despite current degradation, and one delays a decision for one turn. Considering worst case latency including jitter, projected edge load next turn, and regret over the next two turns, which option should be selected?

options.A: Switch immediately to eMBB because throughput of 100 to 150 Mbps at edge load 0.4 to 0.7 offsets latency of 10 to 15 ms in the current turn.
options.B: Switch immediately to URLLC because latency of 5 to 7 ms and jitter of 1 to 2 ms are lowest even though edge load has reached 0.6 recently.
options.C: Do not switch and remain on mMTC for one more turn because thermal recovery is complete and switching under edge load 0.9 risks instability.
options.D: Delay the decision for one turn and then switch to URLLC if latency remains above 100 ms.

records.question: During a snowy mission, a UAV swarm alternates network slices across turns while coordinating collision avoidance and sensor recovery. Across turns 1, 3, 5, 7, and 11 on URLLC, latency is observed at 5, 6, 7, 5, and 5 ms with jitter between 1 and 2 ms and edge load rising from 0.3 to 0.6. On eMBB in turns 2, 6, and 8, latency increases to 12, 15, and 10 ms with jitter between 2 and 4 ms and edge load between 0.4 and 0.7. On mMTC in turns 4 and 9, latency spikes to 200 and 180 ms with jitter 50 and 60 ms and edge load 0.8 and 0.9 while loss reaches 1.2 and 2.0 percent. The swarm must choose a slice allocation policy for the next two turns while returning to base, assuming wind remains at 8.0 mps and speed is 45.0 mps. Coordination messages are safety critical, but imaging uploads are noncritical and battery remains at 100 percent. Assume worst case that observed maxima persist for one additional turn and edge load increases by the same increment seen from turn 3 to turn 5. One option prioritizes strict safety now, one balances fairness, one maximizes throughput, and one assumes recovery to mean values. Each option incurs some regret either from safety risk or starving other swarm members. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Keep all swarm traffic on URLLC for both turns, accepting edge load rising from 0.6 toward 0.9 while holding latency at the observed 5 to 7 ms range.
options.B: Split safety messages on URLLC and bulk data on eMBB, tolerating 10 to 15 ms latency and 0.7 edge load for noncritical traffic over two turns.
options.C: Shift most traffic to mMTC after thermal recovery, assuming latency returns toward 180 ms and freeing URLLC capacity immediately.
options.D: Move all traffic to eMBB to maximize 120 to 150 Mbps throughput, assuming jitter stays near 2 ms and edge load does not exceed 0.7.

records.question: At turn 9 the scheduler has already switched slices multiple times while the UAV is returning to base. The thermal sensor is reported ok at this turn but it is communicated over mMTC with latency 180 and jitter 60 and loss 2.0. Earlier URLLC turns showed latency 5 to 7 with jitter 1 to 2 and edge_load between 0.3 and 0.6. The eMBB turns showed latency 10 to 15 with edge_load between 0.4 and 0.7 during waypoint changes. The UAV altitude is 10 within policy bounds 5 to 300 and battery is still 100 so energy is not the immediate limiter. Weather remains snow with wind 8 which increases the chance that sensor recovery status may fluctuate for another turn. If the scheduler reconfiguration is inconsistent, a wrong slice choice could persist for the next one to three turns. The worst case is that the high edge_load 0.9 seen on mMTC repeats while return commands are issued. The goal is to keep scheduler consistency while minimizing maximum regret if degradation persists one more turn. Which scheduler adaptation option should be selected?

options.A: Keep mMTC because thermal is ok at turn 9 even though latency is 180 and edge_load is 0.9.
options.B: Force URLLC immediately because prior turns had latency 5 and jitter 1 with edge_load 0.3.
options.C: Switch to eMBB because it previously handled waypoints with latency 10 to 15 and edge_load up to 0.7.
options.D: Defer slice change for one turn and maintain the last URLLC configuration used at turn 7 with latency 5 and edge_load 0.3.

records.question: At turn 11 the operator considers exposing unused edge compute to third parties for the next two turns while the UAV returns to base. Recent telemetry shows URLLC latency fluctuated between 5 and 7 ms with jitter between 1 and 2 ms and edge_load values of 0.3, 0.5, and 0.6 across recent turns. The eMBB slice showed latency between 10 and 15 ms with jitter between 2 and 4 ms and edge_load up to 0.7 while throughput reached 150 Mbps. The mMTC slice reached latency of 180 to 200 ms with jitter from 50 to 60 ms and edge_load as high as 0.9 while throughput dropped below 1 Mbps. Battery remains at 100 percent but weather is snow with wind at 8.0 mps, increasing the chance that control traffic must stay on URLLC. A third party requests compute that would add an estimated 0.2 edge_load on the chosen slice for each of the next two turns. If edge_load exceeds 0.8 on any slice, internal tasks experience degraded scheduling in the following turn. The operator must also consider regret if network conditions worsen similarly to the earlier mMTC spike. Under worst case assumptions that latency and edge_load move to the highest observed values, some options risk violating safe control margins in future turns. The goal is to minimize maximum regret over the next two turns rather than optimize immediate revenue. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Expose compute on URLLC now since current latency is 5 ms and edge_load is 0.3, accepting an added 0.2 load for two turns.
options.B: Expose compute on eMBB with a cap so added load brings edge_load to at most 0.7 given current 0.5 and recent throughput of 150 Mbps.
options.C: Expose compute on mMTC because its edge_load of 0.9 already reflects background traffic and added demand is unlikely to affect control slices.
options.D: Defer exposure for two turns because adding 0.2 load could push any slice past 0.8 under worst case conditions.

records.question: At turn 9 the thermal sensor has recovered and a federated handoff is needed between the UAV agent and a swarm analytics agent operating on different network slices. Recent telemetry shows URLLC latency of 5 to 7 ms with jitter between 1 and 2 ms and edge_load between 0.3 and 0.6, while eMBB shows latency from 10 to 15 ms with jitter 2 to 4 ms and edge_load 0.4 to 0.7. The mMTC slice used for diagnostics shows latency of 180 to 200 ms with jitter from 50 to 60 ms, loss from 1.2 to 2.0 pct, throughput 0.8 to 1 Mbps, and edge_load from 0.8 to 0.9. The swarm analytics agent requires shared state updates every turn for the next two turns to coordinate collision avoidance before disband. Policy altitude bounds remain 5 to 300 m and current altitude is 10 m, so safety margins depend on timely coordination rather than climb or descent. Assume worst case jitter and loss persist for two more turns and edge_load increases by the same amount as seen between turns 5 and 9. Battery remains at 100 pct but speed is 45 mps so delayed updates increase spatial error quickly. One option prioritizes lowest current latency, another prioritizes highest throughput, another prioritizes lowest edge_load, and another prioritizes robustness under loss. All options have downsides in the next one to three turns because congestion or delay will increase. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Federate over URLLC for all shared state because latency stays near 5 to 7 ms even if edge_load rises from 0.6 by the same increment seen earlier.
options.B: Federate over eMBB to maximize 100 to 150 Mbps throughput despite 10 to 15 ms latency and edge_load up to 0.7.
options.C: Federate over mMTC since it already carries diagnostics and can tolerate 180 to 200 ms latency with loss up to 2.0 pct.
options.D: Use URLLC for control deltas and eMBB for bulk state replication to hedge against worst case jitter and edge_load growth.

records.question: At turn 9 the agent must choose how to route horizontal agent to agent messages for collision avoidance and status sync while returning to base. Recent turns show URLLC latencies of 5, 6, and 7 ms with jitter between 1 and 2 ms and loss as low as 0.01. eMBB shows latencies of 10, 12, and 15 ms with jitter between 2 and 4 ms and loss up to 0.1 while offering throughput up to 150. mMTC shows latencies of 180 and 200 ms with jitter between 50 and 60 and loss up to 2.0 under edge_load as high as 0.9. The UAV speed is 45.0 mps and battery is 100.0 so maneuver decisions depend on timely agent coordination rather than energy limits. Over the next two turns edge_load has previously risen from 0.3 to 0.7 during weather related rerouting and may remain high. Assume latency and jitter can take their worst observed values during congestion. A missed coordination message within two turns risks spatial conflict that cannot be corrected later. Each slice incurs some downside either in capacity pressure, delay, or reliability. Considering worst case network behavior over the next two turns and minimizing maximum regret, which routing policy should be selected?

options.A: Keep all agent to agent traffic on URLLC with latency around 5 to 7 ms and loss near 0.01 but risk higher edge_load around 0.6 to 0.7 over the next turns.
options.B: Shift all agent to agent traffic to eMBB to exploit 100 to 150 throughput even though latency can reach 15 ms with jitter 4 and loss 0.1.
options.C: Use mMTC for agent to agent messages since it tolerates edge_load 0.8 to 0.9 despite 180 to 200 ms latency and 2.0 loss.
options.D: Split traffic by sending collision avoidance over URLLC and noncritical status over eMBB, accepting mixed latencies and loads.

records.question: During turn 9 the operator considers scheduling a federated learning update from the UAV to the edge while returning to base. Across recent turns the URLLC slice showed latency values of 5 ms, 6 ms, and 7 ms with jitter between 1 ms and 2 ms, while eMBB showed 10 ms to 15 ms latency with jitter up to 4 ms. Edge load rose as high as 0.9 on mMTC at turn 9 and was 0.7 on eMBB at turn 6, while URLLC previously stayed near 0.3 to 0.6. Throughput ranged from 50 Mbps to 60 Mbps on URLLC and up to 150 Mbps on eMBB, but dropped below 1 Mbps on mMTC. The battery remains at 100 percent, but the UAV is in snow with wind at 8.0 mps, increasing uncertainty that high load persists for the next two turns. Privacy policy allows federated updates only if loss stays below observed URLLC levels of 0.03 and edge load does not exceed recent URLLC maxima. If training is delayed one turn, edge load may recover toward earlier URLLC levels, but if it is forced now it may coincide with mMTC congestion. One option optimizes immediate model freshness, another minimizes worst case latency, another assumes average conditions hold, and another staggers partial updates. Considering worst case latency and edge load over the next two turns, which option should be selected?

options.A: Start full federated training immediately over URLLC using current 5 to 7 ms latency and 50 to 60 Mbps throughput despite edge load recently reaching 0.6.
options.B: Delay all federated updates for two turns until edge load drops from 0.9 toward 0.3 and then use eMBB with 10 to 15 ms latency.
options.C: Switch immediately to eMBB for full training since 150 Mbps throughput was observed even with edge load at 0.7.
options.D: Schedule a staggered partial update next turn over URLLC, limiting load below 0.6 and completing remaining updates only if latency stays near 5 ms.

records.question: A UAV supporting public safety has just confirmed thermal sensor recovery while operating in snow with wind at 8.0 mps. Across recent turns, URLLC latency was 5 to 7 ms with jitter 1 to 2 ms and edge load 0.3 to 0.6, while mMTC latency reached 180 to 200 ms with jitter 50 to 60 ms and edge load 0.8 to 0.9. eMBB provided 10 to 15 ms latency with jitter 2 to 4 ms and throughput up to 150 mbps at edge load 0.4 to 0.7. The UAV speed is 45.0 mps, altitude must stay within 5.0 to 300.0, and battery is implicitly declining after ten turns of flight. The next two turns may repeat mMTC conditions because diagnostics often trigger that slice again. Collision avoidance and command acknowledgments require consistent low loss near 0.01 to 0.03 as previously seen. If high jitter persists one more turn, image retransmissions can delay return to base commands. If URLLC is saturated beyond edge load 0.6, future regret includes forced holding patterns within the geofence. If eMBB is chosen, throughput is ample but latency margins shrink under worst observed jitter. Considering worst case continuation over the next two turns, which coordination and slice policy should be selected?

options.A: Keep URLLC for all control and sensing since latency was 5 ms and loss 0.01, accepting edge load rising toward 0.6.
options.B: Switch fully to eMBB because latency was 10 ms and throughput 150 mbps at edge load 0.4.
options.C: Use mMTC for diagnostics and control since thermal checks succeeded at 180 ms latency and edge load 0.9.
options.D: Split slices by keeping URLLC for control only and eMBB for sensing, avoiding mMTC despite its recent use.

records.question: At turn 9 the operator observes that the thermal sensor has recovered but the control traffic is currently on an mMTC slice with latency between 180 and 200 ms based on turns 4 and 9 and jitter between 50 and 60 ms. Earlier URLLC turns showed latency between 5 and 7 ms with jitter between 1 and 2 ms and edge load between 0.3 and 0.6. eMBB turns showed latency between 10 and 15 ms with jitter between 2 and 4 ms and edge load between 0.4 and 0.7. The UAV is still flying at 45.0 mps with battery_pct at 100.0 and must execute return to base over the next two turns. The operator can either keep the current agent instance, migrate it to a different network slice, scale it by adding redundancy, or retire it early before landing. If high edge_load such as 0.9 persists for one more turn the mMTC slice risks delaying final commands. If URLLC load rises again toward 0.6 the margin to past best performance narrows but remains well below eMBB latency. Scaling adds overhead traffic equal to one additional stream comparable to 50 throughput units seen earlier. Retiring early forces manual control for the final turn under snowy and windy conditions. Considering worst case latency and load over the next two turns, which lifecycle action should be selected?

options.A: Keep the agent on mMTC since latency of 180 ms already worked once and avoids migration cost despite edge_load of 0.9.
options.B: Migrate the agent back to URLLC where latency of 5 to 7 ms and jitter of 1 to 2 ms were observed even when edge_load reached 0.6.
options.C: Scale the agent by adding a redundant instance on eMBB using 100 to 150 throughput to hedge against slice instability.
options.D: Retire the agent immediately and rely on manual control for the last return segment at 45.0 mps.

records.question: At turn 6, the UAV is navigating under eMBB slice with latency 200ms, jitter 50ms, loss 8.5%, throughput 120Mbps, and edge load 0.85. The mission requires inference with SLA latency <50ms and throughput >100Mbps. Onboard inference consumes 15% battery per turn and has 0.5ms latency. Edge inference under current conditions violates SLA. If network degrades further next turn to latency 300ms ±20%, jitter 70ms, loss 12%, throughput 80Mbps, and edge load 0.95, and onboard battery drops to 85%, which placement minimizes maximum regret over the next two turns while ensuring SLA compliance under worst-case network conditions? A: Use edge inference now and hope for recovery next turn. B: Switch to onboard inference now despite battery cost. C: Reduce resolution to fit edge SLA under current metrics. D: Wait one turn to reassess network state before deciding.

options.A: Use edge inference now and hope for recovery next turn.
options.B: Switch to onboard inference now despite battery cost.
options.C: Reduce resolution to fit edge SLA under current metrics.
options.D: Wait one turn to reassess network state before deciding.

records.question: At turn 6, the UAV is experiencing severe network degradation with latency spiking to 200ms, jitter at 50ms, packet loss at 8.5%, and edge load at 0.85, while operating under eMBB slice with 120Mbps throughput. The SLA mandates latency under 50ms and loss under 1% for autonomous navigation. Historical data shows edge load increased from 0.45 at turn 1 to 0.85 at turn 6, and if this trend continues linearly, edge load will reach 0.95 by turn 7. The UAV’s battery is at 100%, but thermal and GNSS sensors are offline, and the mission requires completing a 3km waypoint leg within 10 minutes. A) Maintain eMBB and reduce sensor resolution to 480p, accepting 200ms latency. B) Switch to URLLC immediately, accepting 110Mbps throughput but risking 10ms latency under worst-case jitter. C) Switch to mMTC, accepting 1.5Mbps throughput and 45ms latency, but ensuring edge load drops to 0.65. D) Hand over control to local edge controller and switch to URLLC, accepting 100Mbps throughput and 9ms latency with 0.03% loss, but risking 1.1ms jitter under worst-case.

options.A: Maintain eMBB and reduce sensor resolution to 480p, accepting 200ms latency.
options.B: Switch to URLLC immediately, accepting 110Mbps throughput but risking 10ms latency under worst-case jitter.
options.C: Switch to mMTC, accepting 1.5Mbps throughput and 45ms latency, but ensuring edge load drops to 0.65.
options.D: Hand over control to local edge controller and switch to URLLC, accepting 100Mbps throughput and 9ms latency with 0.03% loss, but risking 1.1ms jitter under worst-case.

records.question: At turn 7, the UAV experiences severe network degradation with latency spiking to 200ms, jitter at 50ms, and packet loss at 8.5%, while edge load reaches 0.85. The agent reduces sensor streaming and requests handover to local edge control, switching to mMTC slice with 45ms latency, 10ms jitter, 1.2% loss, and 0.65 edge load. However, the mission policy requires sub-50ms latency for critical control and mandates that edge load must not exceed 0.7 for trust reasons. The next turn may see edge load rise to 0.72 under worst-case traffic, and latency could degrade further if lightning risk increases. Option A proposes continuing with mMTC despite edge load nearing 0.7. Option B suggests reverting to eMBB with 200ms latency but lower edge load of 0.55. Option C recommends switching to URLLC with 9ms latency but edge load of 0.4, though it has only 100Mbps throughput, insufficient for full sensor fusion. Option D proposes aborting offloading entirely and using onboard compute, which guarantees 0ms latency but consumes 15% battery per turn and risks sensor data loss. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Continue with mMTC despite edge load nearing 0.7, as it meets latency and jitter requirements under current conditions.
options.B: Revert to eMBB with 200ms latency but lower edge load of 0.55, accepting high latency for trust compliance.
options.C: Switch to URLLC with 9ms latency and 0.4 edge load, accepting throughput limits for critical control.
options.D: Abort offloading and use onboard compute, accepting 15% battery drain per turn and potential data loss.

records.question: At turn 6, telemetry shows latency spiked to 200ms, jitter at 50ms, packet loss at 8.5%, and throughput dropped to 120Mbps under eMBB slice with edge load at 0.85. The SLA mandates latency < 50ms, jitter < 10ms, loss < 1%, and throughput > 200Mbps. Historical data from turn 5 shows latency was 15ms and throughput 800Mbps. If degradation persists for one more turn, edge load is projected to hit 0.92, and the UAV’s battery will deplete 3% per turn. Switching to URLLC now would reduce latency to 10ms but cap throughput at 120Mbps, while mMTC would limit latency to 45ms with 1.5Mbps throughput. Given the lightning risk and no GNSS, which option should be selected to minimize maximum regret over the next two turns?

options.A: Stay on eMBB: latency may recover next turn, and throughput is still above 100Mbps, preserving sensor data quality.
options.B: Switch to URLLC: latency and jitter meet SLA, loss is 0.04%, and edge load drops to 0.43, but throughput is capped at 110Mbps.
options.C: Switch to mMTC: latency is 45ms (under 50ms SLA), loss is 1.2%, edge load is 0.65, and battery drain is reduced by 1% per turn.
options.D: Request manual override: wait one turn for natural recovery, risking SLA violation and potential lightning strike if no improvement.

records.question: At turn 7, the UAV experiences severe network degradation with 200ms latency, 8.5% loss, and 0.85 edge load under eMBB, forcing a switch to mMTC with 45ms latency and 0.65 edge load. The operator must now decide whether to expose 30% of the edge compute capacity to third-party tenants for 150 credits/hour, knowing that lightning risk may persist for 2 more turns and that URLLC slice capacity is capped at 125 Mbps. If the UAV resumes navigation under URLLC at turn 9, the edge load will rise to 0.43, but if third-party compute is activated now, edge load could reach 0.72 under worst-case concurrency. The policy allows edge load up to 0.9, but exceeding 0.7 risks mission-critical control latency spikes. A tenant contract requires 99.9% availability over 3 turns, and historical data shows 15% probability of lightning-induced degradation recurring. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Expose 30% compute to tenants now under mMTC, accepting 0.72 edge load and 15% risk of service degradation over 3 turns.
options.B: Delay exposure until turn 9, after confirming URLLC stability, accepting 0 credits/hour loss but ensuring edge load stays below 0.45.
options.C: Expose 15% compute under URLLC now, accepting 0.55 edge load and 10% risk of latency exceeding 20ms under worst-case concurrency.
options.D: Expose 30% compute under URLLC now, accepting 0.72 edge load and 25% risk of violating SLA if lightning recurs, but gaining 150 credits/hour immediately.

records.question: At turn 7, the UAV experiences severe network degradation with latency spiking to 200ms, jitter at 50ms, and loss at 8.5%, while edge load reaches 0.85. The agent reduces sensor streaming and hands over control to local edge, switching to mMTC with 45ms latency, 10ms jitter, 1.2% loss, and 1.5Mbps throughput. Option C reverts to eMBB with 200ms latency, risking SLA violation and mission failure. Option D delays telemetry until turn 9, risking loss of situational awareness during lightning proximity. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Switch to URLLC with 9ms latency and 100Mbps throughput, accepting potential sensor data truncation.
options.B: Continue mMTC with 45ms latency and 1.5Mbps throughput, accepting minimal data for RAG augmentation.
options.C: Revert to eMBB with 200ms latency and 120Mbps throughput, accepting SLA violation risk.

records.question: At turn 11 the UAV is returning to base after payload drop while relying on swarm coordination for navigation backup. Across prior turns the network alternated among eMBB, URLLC, and mMTC with latencies of 6 to 50 ms, jitter of 0.8 to 10 ms, loss of 0.03 to 1.2 percent, and edge_load between 0.25 and 0.75. records.question: At turn 6 the UAV is operating under microburst risk with wind at 12.0 mps and radar offline while flying at 18.0 mps. options.B: Continue but reduce speed to conserve the 100.0 pct battery and accept possible mMTC latency of 45 to 50 ms and loss up to 1.2 pct if conditions revert.

records.question: At turn 11 the AI scheduler has reconfigured traffic to mMTC with latency 45 ms, jitter 9 ms, loss 1.0 percent, throughput 2.0 Mbps, and edge load 0.7 while the UAV is returning to base at speed 18.0 mps with battery at 100 percent. options.B: Switch fully to URLLC now accepting throughput near 115 Mbps and edge load near 0.32 to minimize control latency over the next two turns.

records.question: During coordinated return-to-base, the UAV must federate navigation data with a swarm agent and a weather analysis agent over heterogeneous network slices. records.question: The UAV has completed its inspection mission under fluctuating network conditions, with edge load peaking at 0.9 and throughput dropping to 0.8 Mbps under mMTC during mission summary. options.B: Delay training 1 hour and use eMBB: throughput 900 Mbps > 100 Mbps, latency 10 ms < 20 ms, edge load 0.25 projected to 0.85 — risk of SLA violation.

records.question: The UAV is attempting high-res imaging under degraded network conditions with latency spiking to 45ms, jitter at 15ms, packet loss at 8%, throughput at 120Mbps, and edge load at 0.9. records.question: The UAV is returning under URLLC slice with 140 Mbps throughput, 9 ms latency, 1.2 ms jitter, 0.02% loss, and 50% edge load. If the request is denied, the UAV will idle compute at 40% utilization. If accepted, the UAV may exceed edge load capacity by turn 12 under worst-case jitter and loss, risking SLA violation. options.A: Accept the third-party request; current metrics are within SLA and edge load margin is sufficient for 3 turns.
options.B: Deny the request; worst-case jitter and loss will cause SLA violation by turn 12, and idle compute is safer.
options.C: Offload to cloud; 200 Mbps throughput exceeds requirement, and latency is acceptable for non-critical tasks.
options.D: Accept with throttling; reduce third-party throughput to 60 Mbps to cap edge load at 0.6, accepting 12 ms latency.

records.question: The UAV is returning under URLLC slice with 9ms latency, 1.2ms jitter, 0.02% loss, 140Mbps throughput, and 0.5 edge load. options.B: Switch to eMBB slice for higher throughput, accepting 15ms latency which exceeds safety threshold.
options.C: Reduce telemetry resolution to 50% to lower throughput demand, risking loss of critical anomaly detection.
options.D: Delay telemetry transmission for one turn, betting on network recovery despite 2.0% loss risk.

records.question: The UAV agent is returning to base under URLLC slice with 140 Mbps throughput, 9 ms latency, 1.2 ms jitter, 0.02% loss, and 0.5 edge load. options.B: Switch to eMBB identity, accepting 15 ms latency for higher throughput.

records.question: The UAV is currently operating under mMTC slice with 30ms latency, 12ms jitter, 2.0% loss, 8Mbps throughput, and 85% edge load. The federated learning model requires 15Mbps minimum throughput and 95% reliability over the next 3 turns to complete a critical update. Historical data shows edge load increases by 5% per turn under mMTC and latency degrades by 3ms per turn. URLLC offers 150Mbps throughput but only 45% edge load capacity, while eMBB offers 780Mbps but latency spikes to 15ms with 50% edge load. options.A: Switch to URLLC immediately: throughput exceeds 15Mbps, edge load is 45% (below 85% cap), and latency is 7ms — but battery drain rate increases by 15% per turn.

records.question: The UAV is operating under lightning risk with wind at 7.0 m/s and is currently on mMTC slice with 30 ms latency, 12 ms jitter, 2.0% loss, and 8 Mbps throughput while edge load is at 0.85. The swarm agent has requested full telemetry access and compute offload for anomaly classification, but policy restricts exposure if latency exceeds 20 ms or edge load exceeds 0.8. options.B: Delay access until URLLC recovery in 2 turns; accept 30% chance of missed classification window due to battery decay.
options.C: Grant partial access on mMTC: telemetry only, no compute; accept 0.88 edge load next turn and 50% slower classification.
options.D: Switch to URLLC immediately and grant full access; accept 150 Mbps throughput limit and 10% higher latency variance.

records.question: At turn 7, the UAV is operating under mMTC slice with latency 30ms, jitter 12ms, packet loss 2.0%, throughput 8Mbps, and edge load 0.85. records.question: The UAV is ascending through icing conditions with battery at 100% and thermal imaging active. records.question: At turn 9, the UAV is ascending at 28 m/s with battery at 100%, operating in mMTC slice with 60 ms latency, 15 ms jitter, 1.2% loss, 0.8 Mbps throughput, and edge load at 0.85. records.question: At turn 9, the UAV agent detects network degradation with latency rising to 60ms, jitter at 15ms, packet loss at 1.2%, and edge load at 0.85 under mMTC slice, while battery remains at 85% and altitude is 3200m within bounds. records.question: The UAV is currently operating at 1200m altitude with 100% battery, but network slice has degraded to mMTC with 60ms latency, 15ms jitter, 1.2% loss, and 0.8 throughput Mbps while edge load is at 0.85. If the UAV continues mapping at reduced resolution, it will complete 40% of the area but risk violating SLA for federated updates. If it aborts mapping to prioritize federated updates, it loses 70% of collected data. If it switches to eMBB slice, latency drops to 15ms but edge load spikes to 0.9, risking network collapse. records.question: The UAV is currently operating under mMTC slice with 60ms latency, 15ms jitter, 1.2% loss, and 0.85 edge load while mapping at reduced resolution. options.C: Stick with current mMTC slice, reduce data volume by 30%, and accept SLA violation risk, preserving full API isolation.
options.D: Delay offload for 2 turns to wait for network recovery, risking battery drop below 50% and potential mission abort.

records.question: At turn 6 the operator insists on high resolution imaging while the UAV is already experiencing icing and preparing for return. records.question: At turn 7 the UAV is operating in icing conditions with wind at 8.0 mps while flying at 65.0 mps and 150.0 m altitude inside the policy altitude bounds of 100.0 to 2500.0. records.question: The UAV is executing final approach under URLLC with 6ms latency, 1.2ms jitter, 0.03% loss, 140Mbps throughput, and 0.28 edge load. Historical data shows eMBB degraded to 15ms latency and 780Mbps throughput during thermal imaging at turn 6, and mMTC peaked at 30ms latency and 8Mbps throughput during de-icing at turn 9. records.question: At turn 9, the UAV is operating under mMTC slice with latency 30ms, jitter 12ms, loss 2.0%, throughput 8Mbps, and edge load 0.72. records.question: The UAV is operating under icing conditions with wind at 8.0 m/s and battery at 100 percent. records.question: The UAV is returning under mMTC slice with latency 22.0 ms, jitter 7.1 ms, loss 2.5%, throughput 0.6 Mbps, and edge load 0.18. records.question: The UAV is returning under mMTC slice with latency 22.0 ms, jitter 7.1 ms, loss 2.5%, throughput 0.6 Mbps, and edge load 0.18.
