Assume congestion may persist for the next two turns with worst case staying near the observed 0.85 edge load if no action is taken. Switching slices or changing video settings now must remain consistent with the earlier decision to prioritize delivery reliability. A single turn view favors restoring throughput, but a multi turn view penalizes oscillating slices. Under worst case jitter and loss, control safety dominates video quality for landing. Battery and speed indicate the mission will complete within a few turns, so short term regret matters most. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Stay on eMBB at 45 ms latency and 0.85 edge load to preserve 40 Mbps throughput for video, accepting higher jitter this turn.
options.B: Switch to URLLC at 10 ms latency and about 0.35 edge load while keeping reduced video bitrate to fit 50 to 55 Mbps throughput.
options.C: Remain on eMBB but reduce video bitrate only, assuming edge load will fall below 0.65 as in turn 4.
options.D: Alternate between eMBB this turn and URLLC next turn to balance 40 Mbps throughput now with 8 ms latency later.

records.question: At turn 5 the operator considers exposing idle edge compute to third parties while the UAV mission is still active. Recent telemetry shows eMBB latency rose to 45 ms with jitter 15 ms, loss 2.1 percent, throughput 40 Mbps, and edge load 0.85 during congestion. Earlier and later turns show latency as low as 6 to 10 ms and edge load down to 0.25 to 0.35 on URLLC, implying uncertainty across slices. The UAV remains within policy altitude bounds of 10 to 300 meters and still has 100 percent battery, so compute demand from autonomy may persist for several turns. The marketplace offers three exposure modes that reuse existing slices without changing hardware. The operator must consider worst case persistence of the high load for the next two turns rather than assuming recovery. If congestion persists one more turn, control and landing functions may need URLLC with latency near 7 to 10 ms. If recovery occurs, excess capacity appears mainly on URLLC with throughput around 55 to 65 Mbps and edge load near 0.25 to 0.35. Third party jobs are tolerant but add variable load proportional to current edge load. No option is risk free because all add some load or opportunity cost. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Expose third party compute immediately on eMBB because 40 Mbps throughput remains and latency was acceptable earlier at 18 to 25 ms, even though edge load is currently 0.85.
options.B: Expose third party compute on URLLC since latency is 7 to 10 ms and edge load was as low as 0.25 to 0.35 in later turns, assuming recovery continues.
options.C: Delay exposure for two turns and reassess after observing whether edge load falls from 0.85 toward 0.35 while keeping all slices reserved.
options.D: Expose only minimal third party batch jobs on mMTC where edge load is 0.2 and throughput is 1.2 Mbps, accepting high latency of 120 ms.

records.question: At turn 6 the operator considers granting a third party analytics agent access during the final delivery phase. The agent requests either live RGB video, delayed video, metadata only, or compute only access to assist landing verification. Current URLLC metrics show latency between 6 and 10 ms across recent turns, jitter between 0.8 and 2 ms, loss between 0.02 and 0.1 percent, throughput between 52 and 65 Mbps, and edge load between 0.25 and 0.35. Battery is still at 100 percent but speed remains 35 mps and landing will occur within the next two to three turns. Earlier eMBB congestion reached 45 ms latency and 0.85 edge load, indicating plausible regression if load increases again. Policy allows operation within 10 to 300 m altitude but does not mandate third party sharing. If the third party is exposed now, its load is expected to persist for the remaining turns. Under worst case assumptions, latency may rise to the upper observed bound and edge load may return toward the earlier peak. Each exposure option risks either control degradation or loss of post hoc audit value. Which exposure option should be selected to minimize maximum regret over the next two to three turns?

options.A: Grant live RGB video at 60 Mbps over URLLC since current latency is as low as 6 ms and edge load is only 0.28.
options.B: Grant delayed video snapshots at reduced bitrate over eMBB, accepting up to 45 ms latency but preserving full visual data.
options.C: Grant metadata only access such as pose and landing status over URLLC, adding negligible throughput while keeping latency within 10 ms.
options.D: Grant compute only access on the edge, assuming current edge load of 0.25 to 0.35 can absorb the extra processing.

records.question: At turn 6 an immersive AR teleoperation overlay is enabled alongside the existing video feed and control loop. Recent measurements show URLLC latency moving between 6 and 10 ms with jitter between 0.8 and 2 ms and loss between 0.05 and 0.1 over turns 6 to 10, while eMBB previously degraded to 45 ms latency with 15 ms jitter and 2.1 loss at turn 5. Throughput on URLLC is 55 to 65 Mbps with edge_load falling from 0.35 to 0.25, whereas eMBB fell to 40 Mbps with edge_load 0.85. The AR overlay must remain usable for the next two turns even if congestion similar to turn 5 partially returns. Fairness policy requires avoiding starvation of background video, which currently runs at 95 Mbps when unconstrained. If URLLC saturates, edge_load is expected to rebound toward 0.35 within one turn. If eMBB is reintroduced too early, worst case latency may revisit 45 ms based on the last congestion event. mMTC remains available with 120 ms latency, 25 ms jitter, and 1.2 Mbps throughput but low edge_load of 0.2. No option avoids degradation entirely over the next three turns. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Keep all AR and control on URLLC at 55–65 Mbps and leave video suppressed, accepting edge_load possibly returning to 0.35 next turn.
options.B: Move AR to eMBB to regain up to 95 Mbps video throughput despite the prior 45 ms latency and 15 ms jitter seen at turn 5.
options.C: Split AR on URLLC at 55 Mbps and restore reduced video on eMBB accepting a possible loss range of 0.1–2.1 if congestion recurs.
options.D: Shift AR updates to mMTC at 1.2 Mbps to minimize edge_load while keeping control on URLLC at 60 Mbps.

records.question: The UAV is preparing for landing with restored sensors and a stable URLLC slice showing 7ms latency, 1% jitter, 0.05% loss, 200Mbps throughput, and 0.3 edge load. A customer requests immediate LLM fine-tuning using 150Mbps sustained throughput for 3 turns, with SLA requiring <10ms latency and <0.1% loss. Historical data shows edge load increases 0.1 per turn under training load, and worst-case jitter may spike to 3ms. If training begins now, projected edge load in turn 13 will be 0.5, risking violation if wind shear returns. Alternatively, delaying training until turn 14 allows edge load to drop to 0.25 but forfeits 2 turns of revenue. A third option uses eMBB at 800Mbps but with 18ms latency, violating SLA. A fourth option throttles training to 100Mbps to preserve edge load under 0.4, but extends training to 5 turns, risking battery depletion. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Start training now on URLLC: 200Mbps throughput, 7ms latency, edge load 0.3 → projected 0.5 in turn 13, within SLA if no wind shear.
options.B: Delay until turn 14: edge load drops to 0.25, but loses 2 turns of revenue; training completes in 3 turns with 0.35 edge load.
options.C: Use eMBB slice: 800Mbps throughput, but 18ms latency violates SLA; edge load 0.6, risking overload if training extends.
options.D: Throttle to 100Mbps: extends training to 5 turns, edge load stays under 0.4, but battery may drop below 20% by turn 16.

records.question: The UAV is preparing for landing with restored sensors and a planned landing zone, but network conditions are volatile: eMBB slice latency is 18ms with 0.25% loss and 800Mbps throughput at 0.6 edge load, while URLLC slice offers 7ms latency, 0.05% loss, 200Mbps throughput, and 0.3 edge load. Wind shear persists at 8m/s from 240°, and fog reduces visibility, increasing collision risk. The swarm requires sub-10ms latency for coordination, and the landing sequence demands 150Mbps minimum throughput for AR-guided descent. If edge load exceeds 0.85, the system may crash. Over the next two turns, latency may degrade by 20% under fog, and throughput may drop 30% if wind shear intensifies. Which option should be selected to ensure safe landing while preserving AR immersion and minimizing regret across plausible futures?

options.A: Switch to URLLC slice immediately; accept 200Mbps throughput knowing it exceeds the 150Mbps landing minimum, and tolerate 0.3 edge load to preserve sub-10ms latency for swarm coordination.
options.B: Remain on eMBB slice; leverage 800Mbps throughput for AR rendering, accept 18ms latency assuming it will not exceed 21.6ms under fog, and monitor edge load which is currently 0.6 and may rise to 0.72 under stress.
options.C: Switch to mMTC slice temporarily; accept 1.2Mbps throughput and 120ms latency to reduce edge load from 0.6 to 0.4, then switch back to URLLC after one turn when edge load stabilizes.
options.D: Split resources: allocate 50% to URLLC for latency-critical swarm and 50% to eMBB for throughput-intensive AR, accepting 10ms latency and 500Mbps throughput with edge load at 0.75, assuming no further degradation.

records.question: At turn 7 the operator requests confirmation that the mission intent remains feasible after switching to URLLC and reducing sensor resolution. The UAV is flying at 35.0 mps with battery at 100.0 percent and must remain within altitude bounds of 30.0 to 150.0 meters while inside the defined geofence. Current URLLC network telemetry shows latency of 10 ms, jitter of 1.2 ms, loss of 0.05 percent, throughput of 80 Mbps, and edge load of 0.6. The next two turns are expected to include continued object detection and waypoint updates, which previously required 100 to 120 Mbps throughput on URLLC. If edge load increases toward the previously observed 0.8, latency and loss may worsen toward earlier degraded values. Policy requires maintaining control links below 20 ms latency and loss below 1.0 percent for safe navigation. The operator can choose to continue as is, further reduce sensing, change slice again, or slow the UAV while holding altitude. Considering worst case network regression over the next two turns and minimizing maximum regret, which option should be selected?

options.A: Continue on URLLC at 35.0 mps with current sensor reduction, accepting 80 Mbps throughput and edge load 0.6.
options.B: Further reduce sensor resolution to cut throughput below 80 Mbps while staying on URLLC with edge load 0.6.
options.C: Switch back to eMBB to regain 750 to 900 Mbps throughput despite prior latency of 45 ms and loss of 5.0 percent.
options.D: Reduce speed below 35.0 mps and maintain URLLC, accepting higher mission time but keeping latency near 10 ms under higher edge load.

records.question: At turn 7 the UAV has just switched slices after a network degradation was observed. Across turns 1 to 9 the latency has ranged from 8 ms to 45 ms while jitter ranged from 0.5 ms to 12 ms. Throughput has varied from 80 Mbps to 900 Mbps and edge load peaked at 0.8 before easing to 0.55. The UAV is flying at 35 mps at 50 m altitude with policy bounds of 30 m to 150 m and battery at 100 pct. Each slice choice has a downside within the next three turns in either control safety or sensing fidelity. The decision must minimize maximum regret across these plausible futures rather than optimize the current snapshot. Which slice should be selected now?

options.A: Remain on URLLC with 9 to 10 ms latency and 80 to 120 Mbps throughput despite edge load around 0.6, accepting reduced sensing quality over the next two turns.
options.B: Switch back to eMBB aiming for 750 to 900 Mbps throughput since latency was as low as 10 to 15 ms earlier, accepting the risk of a 45 ms spike if congestion returns.
options.C: Adopt a hybrid slice that caps latency near observed URLLC levels while allocating more than 120 Mbps when edge load falls below 0.6.
options.D: Delay any switch and tolerate mMTC like performance near 15 ms latency and 1 Mbps throughput since delivery confirmation is pending.

records.question: At turn 7 the UAV has just switched to URLLC with latency 10 ms, jitter 1.2 ms, loss 0.05 percent, throughput 80 Mbps, and edge load 0.6. Two turns earlier the eMBB slice degraded to 45 ms latency, 12 ms jitter, 5.0 percent loss, throughput 100 Mbps, and edge load 0.8, indicating instability rather than a transient spike. The vehicle is flying at 50 m altitude within policy bounds of 30 to 150 m and at 35 mps with battery still at 100 percent. Sensors include lidar and RGB online while thermal and radar remain offline, so perception redundancy is already reduced. Historical turns show URLLC throughput has varied between 80 and 120 Mbps while edge load ranged from 0.35 to 0.6, creating uncertainty about capacity in the next two turns. Assume object detection and collision avoidance must continue for at least two more turns before landing can be safely initiated. If edge load increases toward its earlier 0.8 level or throughput drops toward 80 Mbps again, control margins narrow even if latency stays near 10 ms. A downgrade decision now trades immediate capability against worst case network and sensor risk over the next two turns. Each option below incurs some downside either in mission efficiency, safety margin, or future recoverability. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Maintain full autonomy on URLLC at 10 ms latency and 80 Mbps throughput because current loss is only 0.05 percent and edge load is 0.6.
options.B: Downgrade to supervised autonomy now, reducing control update rate to fit within 80 Mbps and assuming edge load may rise back to 0.8 within two turns.
options.C: Switch back to eMBB to gain up to 900 Mbps throughput as seen earlier, accepting the prior 45 ms latency and 5.0 percent loss as tolerable for one more turn.
options.D: Continue full autonomy for one more turn and downgrade only if latency exceeds 15 ms or loss exceeds 0.5 percent.

records.question: After the scheduler switched slices at turn 7, the UAV is operating on URLLC with latency fluctuating between 8 and 10 ms as seen across turns 7 to 9, jitter between 0.6 and 1.2 ms, loss between 0.01 and 0.05 percent, throughput between 80 and 90 Mbps, and edge load between 0.4 and 0.6. Earlier at turn 6, eMBB showed 45 ms latency, 12 ms jitter, 5.0 percent loss, 100 Mbps throughput, and edge load of 0.8, which triggered the reconfiguration. The UAV speed is 35.0 mps, battery is at 100.0 percent, and altitude must remain within 30.0 to 150.0 m. The scheduler must decide whether to keep the current configuration or adjust again, assuming the next one to three turns may resemble the worst observed URLLC conditions rather than the best. If edge load returns to 0.6 and loss to 0.05 percent, some actions may queue and affect future task ordering. If instead the system reverts prematurely and the eMBB degradation persists for another turn, telemetry consistency may be lost. Each option below incurs some downside either in throughput headroom, latency margin, or future reconfiguration cost. The decision must minimize maximum regret if poor conditions persist for two more turns. Assume no new sensors come online and no battery recharge occurs. The scheduler must remain consistent with prior adaptations rather than oscillating. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Maintain URLLC with reduced sensor resolution, accepting throughput near 80 Mbps and edge load up to 0.6 to preserve latency between 8 and 10 ms over the next turns.
options.B: Switch back to eMBB to regain up to 100 Mbps throughput, assuming latency improves from the observed 45 ms if congestion clears next turn.
options.C: Switch to mMTC to lower edge load toward 0.3 as seen later, despite throughput dropping to 1 Mbps and latency around 15 ms.
options.D: Alternate between URLLC and eMBB each turn to balance edge load near 0.5 while hoping latency averages below the degraded peak.

records.question: At turn 7 the agent has just switched to URLLC after eMBB degraded at turn 6. Recent network history shows eMBB latency jumped to 45 ms with jitter 12 ms and loss 5.0 while URLLC has ranged between 8 and 10 ms latency with jitter between 0.5 and 1.2 and loss between 0.01 and 0.05. Edge load on URLLC has fluctuated from 0.35 to 0.6 while eMBB peaked at 0.8 and then recovered earlier to 0.25. Throughput on URLLC has stayed between 80 and 120 Mbps whereas eMBB fell to 100 Mbps during degradation but was previously 900 Mbps. Over the next two turns the mission requires consistent telemetry for monitoring and landing rather than high bandwidth sensing. There is uncertainty whether the eMBB degradation persists for one more turn or recovers as earlier. A contradictory decision would be to revert slices now and then switch again if degradation persists. Each option below chooses a slice strategy for the next two turns with an explicit tolerance for worst case metrics. Which option should be selected to minimize maximum regret while remaining consistent with the prior replanning decision?

options.A: Stay on URLLC for the next two turns accepting throughput of 80 to 120 Mbps and edge load up to 0.6 to keep worst case latency near 10 ms.
options.B: Immediately revert to eMBB because it previously delivered 900 Mbps and assume latency returns toward 10 to 15 ms next turn.
options.C: Use URLLC for one turn and preemptively switch back to eMBB on the following turn if edge load exceeds 0.5.
options.D: Switch to mMTC to minimize edge load near 0.3 while accepting throughput of 1 Mbps and latency around 15 ms.

records.question: At turn 7 the agent must choose what network telemetry to expose to a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system while the network has just degraded and been mitigated. Recent turns show eMBB latency jumping from 15 ms to 45 ms with loss rising to 5.0 and edge load reaching 0.8, while URLLC after the switch shows latency between 8 ms and 10 ms with jitter between 0.6 ms and 1.2 ms and throughput between 80 and 100 Mbps. The RAG prompt must be assembled within a tight interactive budget so exposing more fields increases processing time proportionally to throughput consumed. If degradation persists for the next two turns, edge load is expected to increase by at least 0.05 per turn on any slice already above 0.5. If recovery occurs, URLLC throughput may return to 100 Mbps but eMBB loss may remain above 0.2 for one extra turn. Exposing full telemetry including latency, jitter, loss, throughput, and edge load provides maximal context but increases prompt size and risks breaching latency under worst case jitter. Exposing only latency and loss minimizes prompt size but risks missing early congestion signals. Exposing latency, loss, and edge load offers partial congestion awareness with moderate size. Exposing historical eMBB metrics alongside current URLLC metrics adds redundancy but increases processing overhead during high edge load. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Expose full telemetry from the current URLLC slice including latency 8–10 ms, jitter up to 1.2 ms, loss up to 0.05, throughput 80–100 Mbps, and edge load 0.6.
options.B: Expose only latency and loss from the current URLLC slice using latency 8–10 ms and loss 0.01–0.05 to minimize prompt size.
options.C: Expose latency, loss, and edge load from the current URLLC slice using latency 8–10 ms, loss 0.01–0.05, and edge load 0.6.
options.D: Expose current URLLC telemetry plus historical eMBB latency 15–45 ms, loss up to 5.0, and edge load up to 0.8 for comparison.

records.question: At turn 7 the UAV agent must decide how to federate perception data with a swarm agent and a logistics agent while the network has recently degraded. Earlier eMBB latency rose to 45 ms with 5.0 percent loss and edge load 0.8 at turn 6, while URLLC around turns 7 to 9 shows latency between 8 and 10 ms, loss between 0.01 and 0.05 percent, throughput between 80 and 100 Mbps, and edge load between 0.4 and 0.6. The swarm agent requires timely collision updates every turn, while the logistics agent only needs delivery confirmation similar to turn 10 where throughput was 1 Mbps and latency 15 ms. The UAV speed is 35 mps and altitude must remain within the policy bounds of 30 to 150 m over the next two turns. If degradation persists for two more turns, worst case latency should be assumed equal to the highest observed in the recent history. If edge load increases by the same amount seen from turn 7 to 8, compute the projected load for the next turn when planning federation. The decision must minimize maximum regret across the next three turns rather than optimize only the current turn. Sharing too much data risks missed collision avoidance, while sharing too little risks delayed mission confirmation. Considering these constraints and uncertainties, which interoperability option should be selected?

records.question: At turn 7 the UAV has rgb and lidar sensors operational while thermal and radar remain offline, and the network has just switched to URLLC with latency 10 ms, jitter 1.2 ms, loss 0.05 pct, throughput 80 Mbps, and edge load 0.6. The next turn may see either recovery to turn 2 levels or further degradation to 35 ms latency and 5% loss. Which option should be selected to minimize maximum regret over the next two turns while preserving federated training integrity?

options.A: Continue on eMBB with current settings, assuming recovery to turn 2 performance by turn 6.
options.B: Switch immediately to URLLC slice despite lower throughput, ensuring latency and loss SLAs are met.
options.C: Delay federated training for one turn to observe network recovery, risking missed synchronization window.
options.D: Split federated updates across both slices, allocating 60% to eMBB and 40% to URLLC to balance throughput and latency.

records.question: At turn 6, the UAV switches to URLLC slice after observing eMBB degradation: latency rose from 15ms to 25ms, jitter from 5ms to 12ms, loss from 0.3% to 2.1%, throughput dropped from 700Mbps to 400Mbps, and edge load increased from 0.6 to 0.85. The URLLC slice now provides 9ms latency, 2ms jitter, 0.08% loss, 150Mbps throughput, and 0.4 edge load. A third-party logistics agent requests access to real-time telemetry and trajectory updates for route optimization, citing SLA of 10ms latency and 99.9% reliability. However, URLLC capacity is constrained, and edge load may rise to 0.55 if the agent is granted full access. Historical data shows that edge load above 0.6 triggers 30% latency degradation within 2 turns. The agent’s trust score is 0.78, below the 0.85 threshold for unrestricted access. The UAV must decide exposure level under worst-case assumptions: if edge load exceeds 0.6 in turn 7, latency could spike to 13ms, violating SLA. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Grant full telemetry and trajectory access; current URLLC latency is 9ms, below SLA, and trust score is above 0.75.
options.B: Grant read-only telemetry with 1s sampling delay; restrict trajectory to coarse waypoints; edge load capped at 0.45 to avoid SLA violation risk.
options.C: Deny all access; URLLC throughput is only 150Mbps, insufficient for real-time streaming, and trust score is below 0.85.
options.D: Grant full access but throttle to 50Mbps; edge load projected at 0.55, which is below 0.6, so SLA should hold under mean conditions.

records.question: The UAV agent has completed delivery under URLLC slice with 6ms latency, 1% loss, and 180Mbps throughput, while edge load is at 0.28. Historical data shows eMBB slice degraded from 12ms to 25ms latency and 850Mbps to 400Mbps throughput over turns 1–5, with edge load rising from 0.45 to 0.85. URLLC slice maintained sub-10ms latency but throughput capped at 180Mbps. The thermal sensor remains offline, and sensor fusion is active. Wind speed is 12m/s with 240-degree direction, and altitude bounds are 10–120m. If the next mission requires high-throughput imaging and the edge load is projected to rise by 0.1 per turn under URLLC, while eMBB may recover to 700Mbps but with 15ms latency and 0.6 edge load, which option should be selected to minimize maximum regret over the next three turns under worst-case uncertainty of 20% latency variance and 10% throughput degradation?

options.A: Migrate to eMBB slice immediately, accepting 15ms latency and 0.6 edge load, assuming recovery holds and thermal sensor remains offline.
options.B: Retire the current agent and instantiate a new one with thermal sensor redundancy, accepting 3-turn downtime and 0.3 edge load overhead.
options.C: Stay on URLLC slice, accepting 180Mbps throughput cap and projected edge load of 0.58 in three turns, with 20% latency variance risk.
options.D: Switch to mMTC slice for low-cost operation, accepting 50ms latency and 1.2Mbps throughput, with 0.2 edge load, ignoring imaging requirements.

records.question: The UAV has completed delivery and is now idle with battery at 82%, operating under URLLC slice with 6ms latency, 1ms jitter, 0.01% loss, 180Mbps throughput, and 0.28 edge load. A customer requests immediate LLM fine-tuning requiring 250Mbps sustained throughput for 3 turns, with SLA allowing max 10ms latency and 0.1% loss. Historical data shows URLLC degrades to 150Mbps throughput under 0.4 edge load with 12ms latency during wind gusts above 10m/s, which are forecasted to persist for 2 more turns. eMBB currently offers 900Mbps but has 0.85 edge load and 25ms latency, with risk of 400Mbps drop if load exceeds 0.9. mMTC is available at 1.2Mbps but violates SLA. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Accept on URLLC: current 180Mbps is below 250Mbps requirement but may suffice if wind subsides; SLA latency and loss are met.
options.B: Accept on eMBB: 900Mbps exceeds requirement, but 25ms latency violates SLA; edge load may spike to 0.91 under training load, risking 400Mbps drop.
options.C: Defer until turn 14: wait for wind to subside, reducing URLLC load to 0.25 and restoring 200Mbps; training can then run on URLLC with 8ms latency.
options.D: Accept on mMTC: 1.2Mbps is far below requirement but incurs no edge load; SLA violated, but training may complete in 10 turns with retries.

records.question: The UAV is completing an immersive AR-guided delivery under dust conditions with wind at 12 m/s from 240 degrees, currently at 20m altitude with 100% battery and thermal sensor offline. Network slice is URLLC with 6ms latency, 1ms jitter, 0.01% loss, 180 Mbps throughput, and 0.28 edge load. Historical data shows eMBB degraded from 12ms to 25ms latency over 5 turns with edge load rising to 0.85. URLLC has maintained sub-10ms latency but throughput capped at 180 Mbps. A new AR overlay requires 250 Mbps throughput for 3D reconstruction, but URLLC cannot support it. eMBB could support it but risks latency exceeding 20ms in next turn under current wind and dust trends. mMTC is available but has 50ms latency and 1.2 Mbps throughput. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Stay on URLLC: latency and reliability are critical for AR safety; accept degraded 3D reconstruction quality due to 180 Mbps cap.
options.B: Switch to eMBB: 250 Mbps meets throughput requirement; assume wind/dust stabilize and latency stays under 20ms for next 2 turns.
options.C: Switch to mMTC: use low-bandwidth AR mode; prioritize battery conservation and edge load reduction to 0.2; accept 50ms latency.
options.D: Hybrid mode: split AR stream — use URLLC for control plane (6ms latency) and eMBB for media plane (250 Mbps); risk edge load exceeding 0.9 if eMBB degrades further.

records.question: At turn 5, network telemetry shows eMBB slice latency spiked to 25ms with 12ms jitter and 2.1% packet loss, while edge load reached 0.85, exceeding the 0.80 safety threshold. The UAV is at 20m altitude with 100% battery, and thermal sensor remains offline. Policy allows switching to URLLC, which historically maintains latency under 10ms but caps throughput at 150Mbps, insufficient for real-time thermal streaming if restored. If degradation persists into turn 6, edge load may hit 0.92, risking SLA violation. Switching now incurs 1.5s handover delay but guarantees sub-10ms latency for next 3 turns. Waiting risks mission failure if loss exceeds 3% or latency breaches 30ms. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Switch to URLLC immediately to enforce latency SLA, accepting throughput limitation and 1.5s handover delay, as worst-case edge load projection exceeds 0.90 by turn 6.
options.B: Maintain eMBB and activate sensor fusion to compensate for thermal failure, assuming network degradation is transient and will recover by turn 6 as seen in prior cycles.
options.C: Switch to mMTC to reduce edge load to 0.2, accepting 50ms latency and 0.5% loss, which violates latency SLA but preserves battery by minimizing retransmissions.
options.D: Request manual override to delay decision until turn 6 telemetry, accepting 25% probability of SLA breach if degradation worsens, but preserving full throughput for potential sensor recovery.

records.question: During a mid-mission transit, the agent’s original intent was continuous high-fidelity sensing while maintaining stable coordination links. From turns 1 to 4 the network used eMBB then URLLC with latencies of 12, 11, 8, and 7 ms and edge_load rising from 0.35 to 0.43. At turn 5 and 6 eMBB latency increased to 15 and 16 ms with jitter 3.2 and 3.5 ms and edge_load 0.52 and 0.58 while the UAV speed remained 22 mps and battery_pct was 100. Turn 7 showed a sharp switch to mMTC with latency 45 ms, jitter 12 ms, loss 2.1 percent, throughput 1.2 Mbps, and edge_load 0.78. At turn 8 the user switched to low-bandwidth mode and the slice returned to URLLC with latency 9 ms, jitter 1.1 ms, throughput 110 Mbps, and edge_load 0.65. By turn 9 the agent resumed high-fidelity sensing on eMBB at 13 ms latency and edge_load 0.48. The uncertainty is whether the degradation pattern from turn 7 can recur for one or two more turns, giving a plausible latency range of 7 to 45 ms and edge_load range of 0.48 to 0.78. An intent drift would be indicated if actions prioritize sensing quality over sustained robustness given this uncertainty and the prior need to downshift modes. Each option below interprets the same telemetry but projects different worst-case outcomes over the next two turns. Which option should be selected as the correct detection of intent drift?

options.A: No drift is present because the return to 13 ms latency and 0.48 edge_load at turn 9 restores conditions similar to turns 1 and 2.
options.B: Drift is present because resuming high-fidelity sensing on eMBB at turn 9 ignores the prior 45 ms and 0.78 edge_load event that could recur within two turns.
options.C: No drift is present because switching back to eMBB maximizes throughput from 110 to 820 Mbps and the battery is still 100 percent.
options.D: Drift is present only if latency exceeds 16 ms again, so the 13 ms reading at turn 9 rules it out for now.

records.question: At turn 9 the UAV has resumed high‑fidelity sensing while flying at 22.0 mps with battery at 100.0 percent inside altitude bounds of 10.0 to 150.0 meters. The current eMBB slice shows latency 13 ms, jitter 2.1 ms, loss 0.15 percent, throughput 820 Mbps, and edge load 0.48. Earlier in the same flight a transient collapse occurred at turn 7 with mMTC latency 45 ms, jitter 12 ms, loss 2.1 percent, throughput 1.2 Mbps, and edge load 0.78. URLLC performance observed at turns 4 and 8 ranged from latency 7 to 9 ms, jitter 0.8 to 1.1 ms, loss 0.01 to 0.03 percent, throughput 110 to 135 Mbps, and edge load 0.43 to 0.65. The operator expects two more turns of thermal sensing before mission end and cannot assume the degradation will not recur. High‑fidelity sensing benefits from throughput but control safety degrades sharply if latency spikes above the mMTC episode. Edge load has been rising and may again exceed 0.65 under worst‑case contention. A hybrid slice would split traffic but inherits partial edge load exposure from both profiles. Selecting a slice now must minimize worst‑case regret across the next two turns rather than optimize the current snapshot. Which slice should be selected?

options.A: Stay on eMBB to preserve 820 Mbps throughput with current 13 ms latency and accept risk if edge load rises from 0.48 toward 0.78.
options.B: Switch fully to URLLC to lock latency near 7 to 9 ms even though throughput drops to about 110 to 135 Mbps and edge load can reach 0.65.
options.C: Adopt a hybrid slice that keeps sensing on eMBB while control uses URLLC, assuming current edge load 0.48 remains stable.
options.D: Preemptively downgrade sensing and remain on eMBB, betting that the mMTC‑like collapse was a one‑turn anomaly.

records.question: At turn 7 the agent must decide what network telemetry and mission knowledge to expose to a RAG prompt while anticipating unstable connectivity. Recent turns show latency of 15 ms and 16 ms on eMBB, then a spike to 45 ms on mMTC, followed by recovery to 9 ms on URLLC. Throughput varied from 780 and 750 Mbps down to 1.2 Mbps, then up to 110 Mbps, while edge load rose from 0.52 and 0.58 to 0.78 before dropping to 0.65. Loss increased from 0.3 and 0.4 percent to 2.1 percent during degradation. The UAV is flying at 22.0 mps with battery at 100.0 percent and altitude 25.0 m, so mission continuation is not energy constrained. The RAG system can include raw thermal frames, summarized thermal metadata, full network time series, or only current-slice indicators. If degradation persists one more turn, worst observed network conditions may repeat before recovery. If recovery persists, higher fidelity data would improve downstream reasoning but increase prompt latency. The decision must minimize maximum regret across both futures rather than optimize the current turn. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Include raw thermal frames and full network time series because current URLLC latency of 9 ms and throughput of 110 Mbps appear sufficient.
options.B: Include summarized thermal metadata plus recent network time series since this fits within throughput observed above 1.2 Mbps and tolerates latency swings up to 45 ms.
options.C: Include only current-slice indicators and drop thermal data entirely to avoid any impact when edge load returns to 0.78.
options.D: Include raw thermal frames but exclude network metrics because battery is 100.0 percent and altitude 25.0 m indicates low mission risk.

records.question: At turn 7 the agent observes severe network degradation while coordinating horizontally with another UAV agent for path updates. Across recent turns, observed latency has ranged from 7 ms on URLLC to 45 ms on mMTC, with throughput ranging from 1.2 Mbps to 870 Mbps and edge load rising from 0.41 to 0.78. Jitter increased from below 1 ms to 12 ms and loss rose from 0.01 percent to 2.1 percent during the worst turn. The agent must select a routing and QoS policy for the next two turns of agent to agent coordination. If degradation persists for one more turn, worst case latency and loss must still allow timely exchange of path corrections. If recovery occurs as previously observed, the policy should not create excessive future congestion or starvation. URLLC offers low latency around 7 to 9 ms but throughput near 110 to 135 Mbps with edge load up to 0.65. eMBB offers high throughput near 820 Mbps with latency around 13 to 16 ms and edge load near 0.48 to 0.58. mMTC shows very low throughput at 1.2 Mbps with latency at 45 ms and edge load 0.78. Considering worst case continuation of turn 7 conditions and regret over the next two turns, which option should be selected?

options.A: Route all agent to agent traffic over URLLC immediately, accepting throughput near 110 Mbps and edge load 0.65 to guarantee sub 10 ms latency if the next turn matches turn 8.
options.B: Keep routing on eMBB with latency around 15 ms and throughput around 820 Mbps, assuming degradation was transient and will not exceed the loss of 0.3 percent seen earlier.
options.C: Fallback to mMTC for resilience since it tolerates edge load 0.78, despite 45 ms latency and 1.2 Mbps throughput.
options.D: Use eMBB for bulk state exchange and reserve URLLC only for critical agent messages, limiting URLLC load near 0.65 while avoiding mMTC worst case.

records.question: At turn 7 the XR operator observes a switch to mMTC with latency 45 ms, jitter 12 ms, loss 2.1 percent, throughput 1.2 Mbps, and edge load 0.78 during an immersive thermal overlay. Earlier eMBB telemetry showed latency values spanning 11 to 16 ms, jitter from 1.8 to 3.5 ms, loss from 0.05 to 0.4 percent, throughput between 750 and 870 Mbps, and edge load rising as high as 0.58. URLLC operation in adjacent turns delivered latency between 7 and 9 ms, jitter between 0.7 and 1.1 ms, throughput between 110 and 135 Mbps, and edge load between 0.4 and 0.65. The immersive session requires sustained high throughput for visual fidelity but becomes unusable if worst case latency exceeds recent mMTC levels for two consecutive turns. The edge scheduler must choose a slice and resource bias now, assuming degradation could persist for up to two more turns and edge load may drift back toward 0.78. One option maximizes immediate fidelity by returning to eMBB despite prior load growth. Another option locks URLLC to cap latency but constrains throughput relative to past eMBB highs. A third option keeps mMTC to protect the edge but sacrifices immersion quality. The fourth option dynamically alternates slices each turn, assuming recovery like that seen by turn 9. Considering worst case latency, throughput needs, and regret over the next two turns, which option should be selected?

options.A: Return immediately to eMBB with observed latency 11 to 16 ms and throughput up to 870 Mbps, accepting edge load risk toward 0.58 and above.
options.B: Stay on URLLC with latency 7 to 9 ms and throughput 110 to 135 Mbps, tolerating edge load up to 0.65 over the next turns.
options.C: Remain on mMTC at 45 ms latency and 1.2 Mbps throughput to minimize additional edge load near 0.78.
options.D: Alternate URLLC and eMBB each turn assuming recovery like the shift from turn 7 to turn 9 with edge load dropping toward 0.48.

records.question: At turn 7 the monitoring system flags a potential network attack as the slice shifts to mMTC with latency 45 ms, jitter 12 ms, loss 2.1 pct, throughput 1.2 Mbps, and edge load 0.78. In earlier turns on eMBB latency ranged from 11 to 16 ms with loss at most 0.4 pct and edge load up to 0.58, while URLLC showed latency between 7 and 9 ms with edge load from 0.41 to 0.65. Security automation must choose a response that limits damage if the mMTC degradation persists for up to two more turns. The system also observes that throughput on URLLC is only 110 to 135 Mbps compared to 750 to 870 Mbps on eMBB. A false positive isolation has a cost if recovery like turn 8 occurs, but a missed attack has a cost if mMTC metrics recur. Worst case reasoning assumes latency stays at 45 ms and edge load remains near 0.78 next turn. A myopic action could optimize the current turn but increase regret if the anomaly repeats. Another option could appear safe at average metrics but fail if loss stays above 2 pct. The automation must minimize maximum regret over the next three turns under these uncertainties. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Immediately isolate the node and force URLLC traffic only, accepting throughput near 110 Mbps and edge load around 0.65 despite recovery seen at turn 8.
options.B: Keep current routing on mMTC since 1.2 Mbps is sufficient for control and assume latency will return toward 16 ms as seen before.
options.C: Rate limit traffic and shift noncritical flows to eMBB, tolerating latency up to 15 ms and edge load near 0.58 while monitoring loss.
options.D: Quarantine sensors and pause data transmission until loss drops below 0.4 pct as observed earlier, even if latency remains 45 ms.

records.question: The mission began as a survey with ascent approval and stable eMBB and URLLC performance at latencies between 8 and 12 ms and edge load near 0.35 to 0.42. By turn 6 the user explicitly initiated collision avoidance, and at turn 7 the agent executed an evasion maneuver while the network shifted to mMTC with 50 ms latency, 10 ms jitter, 1.2 percent loss, 1.5 Mbps throughput, and edge load 0.78. At turn 8 the user reduced data streaming due to network conditions while mMTC latency rose to 55 ms and edge load increased to 0.82. At turn 9 the agent stated resume survey after clearance and the slice returned to URLLC with 9 ms latency and edge load 0.41. The altitude policy remained a range from 1000 to 7000 throughout, so vertical intent did not constrain interpretation. The original survey intent implies sustained high throughput near 800 to 900 Mbps as seen in turns 1, 2, and 10, which was incompatible with the mMTC phase. If mMTC conditions persist one more turn, survey sensing would remain degraded, but if URLLC recovery is stable, survey could resume with lower throughput around 115 Mbps. The uncertainty lies in whether the network degradation was transient or reflects a sustained operational shift driven by collision avoidance. A myopic view would trust the immediate recovery at turn 9, while a worst case assumes one to two more turns of mMTC-level constraints. Considering regret over the next two turns, which interpretation of intent should be selected?

options.A: Classify the behavior as no intent drift because URLLC latency returned to 9 ms and edge load dropped to 0.41 at turn 9, matching earlier survey conditions.
options.B: Classify the behavior as a temporary disturbance because collision avoidance ended and altitude bounds of 1000 to 7000 were never violated.
options.C: Classify the behavior as intent drift toward safety prioritization because mMTC latency of 50 to 55 ms, throughput near 1.2 to 1.5 Mbps, and edge load up to 0.82 indicate a sustained shift that could persist another turn.
options.D: Classify the behavior as network-only drift because throughput recovered to 115 Mbps on URLLC, which is sufficient for minimal survey continuity.

records.question: At turn 9 the UAV resumes survey after clearance while previously experiencing rapid slice changes during turns 7 and 8. The current slice is URLLC with latency 9 ms, jitter 1.1 ms, loss 0.03 percent, throughput 115 Mbps, and edge load 0.41. In the last three turns, URLLC latency ranged from 7 to 10 ms and edge load ranged from 0.38 to 0.45, showing uncertainty that could persist into the next two turns. Earlier eMBB showed latency between 11 and 13 ms with throughput 800 to 900 Mbps and edge load around 0.32 to 0.36. mMTC previously showed latency 50 to 55 ms, jitter 10 to 12 ms, loss 1.2 to 1.5 percent, and edge load up to 0.82 during evasive maneuvers. The UAV speed remains 28 mps and battery is 100 percent, so mission endurance is not immediately constrained. Swarm coordination just completed, but another coordination update may occur within one to two turns if icing or wind at 8.5 mps worsens. If degradation persists for two more turns, the decision should minimize worst case regret rather than optimize current throughput. A myopic choice might favor high bandwidth, while another might favor ultra low latency without considering load saturation risk. One option appears acceptable now but would fail if latency drifts to the observed upper bound. Considering the next three turns and worst case network behavior, which option should be selected?

options.A: Switch immediately to eMBB, accepting latency around 11 to 13 ms to gain 800 Mbps throughput while edge load stays near 0.36.
options.B: Remain on URLLC despite latency possibly reaching 10 ms and edge load 0.45 to preserve coordination stability over the next two turns.
options.C: Switch to mMTC since latency already rose once to 50 ms and throughput needs are reduced to 1.2 Mbps.
options.D: Alternate slices next turn by moving to eMBB now and planning URLLC again if latency exceeds 12 ms.

records.question: During turn 8 the UAV is operating on the mMTC slice with latency at 55 ms, jitter at 12 ms, loss at 1.5 percent, throughput at 1.2 Mbps, and edge load at 0.82. One turn earlier on the same slice the latency was 50 ms, jitter 10 ms, loss 1.2 percent, throughput 1.5 Mbps, and edge load 0.78. Earlier URLLC operation showed latency between 7 and 10 ms with edge load between 0.38 and 0.45, but the current mission phase may keep mMTC for up to three more turns. The battery is still 100 percent and speed is 28.0 mps, so energy is not the limiting factor. Assume the recent increase in edge load of 0.04 per turn could persist for the next two turns under icing and swarm coordination. Assume worst case latency follows the observed range and reaches the highest recently observed value whenever edge load exceeds 0.8. The objective is to reduce autonomy level before a communication driven control degradation occurs, not after. A single turn recovery back to URLLC is possible but not guaranteed based on turn 7 to 9 behavior. Each option below sacrifices capability immediately but may avoid larger loss later. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Maintain current autonomy and sensing on mMTC since 55 ms latency and 1.2 Mbps throughput are still workable for one turn.
options.B: Switch immediately to URLLC to cut latency back near 10 ms even though edge load was already 0.45 on that slice.
options.C: Reduce autonomy by disabling swarm coordination and high rate streaming now, accepting reduced capability while keeping mMTC.
options.D: Delay any change until the next turn to see if edge load falls back toward 0.78 as it did previously.

records.question: At turn 8 the UAV is in icing conditions with wind 8.5 mps while flying at 28.0 mps inside altitude bounds of 1000.0 to 7000.0. Network telemetry over recent turns shows latency ranging from 7 to 55 ms, jitter from 0.9 to 12 ms, loss from 0.01 to 1.5 percent, throughput from 1.2 to 900 Mbps, and edge load from 0.32 to 0.82. The system just reduced data streaming because the slice is mMTC with 55 ms latency, 12 ms jitter, 1.5 percent loss, 1.2 Mbps throughput, and 0.82 edge load. In earlier turns the slice recovered to URLLC with 9 ms latency, 1.1 ms jitter, 0.03 percent loss, and 0.41 edge load, but this recovery has only lasted one turn before. Assume the worst case that the next one to two turns revert to the highest latency and edge load already observed. The mission goal favors survey continuity but the task requires degrading autonomy before a failure occurs rather than after. Battery is still at 100.0 percent so energy is not yet limiting, but icing increases control risk if command updates are delayed. A myopic choice would optimize the current URLLC snapshot, while another choice barely fits within altitude policy but stresses networking again. Each option below degrades capability differently and all incur some loss of mission quality within the next three turns. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Maintain full autonomous survey with swarm coordination since URLLC previously achieved 9 ms latency and 0.41 edge load, accepting the risk of reverting to 55 ms if it happens.
options.B: Preemptively downgrade to supervised autonomy with reduced maneuver aggressiveness and keep altitude constant within 1000.0 to 7000.0, assuming latency may return to 55 ms and edge load to 0.82.
options.C: Switch back to URLLC and restore higher data streaming because throughput was once 130 Mbps and loss 0.01 percent, relying on another rapid recovery.
options.D: Descend toward the lower bound at 1000.0 m to reduce icing exposure while keeping full autonomy, even if mMTC latency of 55 ms and jitter of 12 ms persist.

records.question: At turn 9 the UAV has resumed the survey after clearance while weather remains icing with wind at 8.5 mps and the aircraft is flying at 28.0 mps within altitude bounds of 1000.0 to 7000.0. Network history shows URLLC latency as low as 7 to 10 ms earlier but mMTC spikes reached 55 ms with jitter up to 12 ms and edge load up to 0.82 in the immediately preceding turns. Loss ranged from 0.01 to 1.5 percent across slices, and throughput collapsed from 130 Mbps to 1.2 Mbps during congestion. At turn 9 the link returned to URLLC with 9 ms latency, 1.1 ms jitter, 0.03 percent loss, and edge load 0.41, but there is uncertainty whether mMTC congestion recurs next turn. The mission policy allows continued operation within the same altitude band but icing increases control risk if network degradation persists for more than one turn. If congestion recurs, worst case latency could revert to the prior observed maximum while edge load could again exceed 0.78, stressing coordination. Over the next two turns, a conservative continuation should minimize maximum regret between aborting too early and continuing into degraded control. One option prioritizes current low latency, another hedges against worst case recurrence, another assumes mean conditions persist, and another changes slices aggressively. Each option incurs some downside in safety margin, data quality, or coordination risk within one to three turns. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Continue immediately on URLLC since current latency is 9 ms and edge load is 0.41, accepting the risk that congestion like 55 ms latency does not return.
options.B: Continue the mission but maintain reduced streaming and conservative maneuvering to tolerate up to the previously observed 55 ms latency and 0.82 edge load over the next two turns.
options.C: Switch back to eMBB to exploit 800 to 900 Mbps throughput seen earlier, assuming loss near 0.1 percent and ignoring the recent mMTC spikes.
options.D: Abort the survey now despite URLLC recovery because any nonzero chance of returning to 1.5 percent loss and 12 ms jitter is unacceptable.

records.question: At turn 9 the agent has clearance to resume the survey after an evasion, but recent turns show volatile network conditions. Earlier URLLC operation showed latency between 7 and 10 ms with edge load between 0.38 and 0.45, while mMTC during evasion degraded to 50 to 55 ms latency with edge load up to 0.82. eMBB at the beginning and end showed stable latency between 11 and 13 ms and edge load around 0.32 to 0.36 with much higher throughput. The user already reduced streaming at turn 8 due to network stress, and the policy altitude bounds remain 1000 to 7000 with the UAV currently near 1200. The decision now must be consistent with resuming survey while avoiding a flip flop in network and sensing strategy across the next two turns. If congestion persists for one more turn, a return to high edge load would risk another forced reduction. If conditions instead recover as at turn 9, overly conservative choices incur lost survey quality and future replans. Battery remains at 100 percent so energy is not the binding constraint. The agent must pick the least bad option that minimizes worst case regret over the next one to three turns under uncertain edge load. Which option should be selected?

options.A: Immediately switch back to full survey streaming on URLLC using observed 9 ms latency and 0.41 edge load to maximize safety and consistency with turn 9.
options.B: Stay on mMTC with reduced streaming because it tolerated 0.82 edge load before and avoids another slice change even if latency stays near 55 ms.
options.C: Gradually restore survey by selecting eMBB with the already reduced streaming, using its 11 to 13 ms latency and 0.32 to 0.36 edge load while monitoring one more turn.
options.D: Hold all survey actions for another turn despite clearance, maintaining reduced streaming and current slice to eliminate immediate network risk.

records.question: At turn 8 the UAV must choose how to federate data with a swarm agent after mMTC degradation while preparing to resume coordinated survey. The current network shows latency 55 ms, jitter 12 ms, loss 1.5 percent, throughput 1.2 Mbps, and edge load 0.82, while earlier URLLC coordination in turns 5 and 6 had latency between 7 and 10 ms, loss between 0.01 and 0.04 percent, and edge load between 0.38 and 0.45. The UAV speed is 28 mps and battery is 100 percent, so endurance is not yet limiting but collision risk scales with delayed sharing. Swarm formation requires timely exchange of state vectors and intent updates every turn, but full sensor sharing is optional. Historical behavior shows edge load dropped to 0.41 by turn 9 only after separation was confirmed, so recovery is uncertain if congestion persists one more turn. Loss and jitter have fluctuated across turns, so worst case coordination must tolerate the highest observed values. If federation is too heavy, mMTC edge load above 0.78 risks another turn of reduced throughput. If federation is too light, delayed intent propagation could cause regret in the next two turns when resuming survey. Which interoperability option should be selected to minimize maximum regret over the next one to three turns?

options.A: Maintain full bi directional sensor and telemetry federation over URLLC assuming latency stays near 9 ms and edge load near 0.41 as in turn 9.
options.B: Suspend all swarm data sharing for one turn to wait for edge load to fall below 0.78 before re enabling coordination.
options.C: Federate only low rate state and intent messages over URLLC while keeping reduced local streaming at 1.2 Mbps until loss drops below 0.04 percent.
options.D: Shift all swarm coordination to mMTC with reduced fidelity since throughput of 1.2 Mbps is currently available.

records.question: During turn 6 the UAV is executing collision avoidance while coordinating with a swarm agent over URLLC. In the prior three turns URLLC latency ranged from 7 to 10 ms, jitter from 0.9 to 1.5 ms, loss from 0.01 to 0.04 percent, throughput from 100 to 130 Mbps, and edge load from 0.38 to 0.45. records.question: At turn 7 the monitoring system flags a possible network-layer anomaly after the slice shifts to mMTC with latency 52 ms, jitter 15 ms, loss 2.1 pct, throughput 0.9 Mbps, and edge load 0.8. A single-turn view favors immediate throughput recovery, but a multi-turn view must minimize worst-case regret if degradation continues. One option prioritizes URLLC failover, another throttles traffic further on mMTC, another isolates the edge node, and another performs selective rate limiting with delayed isolation. options.B: Continue on mMTC and further throttle data below the current 0.9 Mbps to reduce edge load from 0.8 despite latency already at 52 ms and loss at 2.1 pct.
options.C: Isolate the mMTC edge node immediately due to the rise from 0.75 to 0.8 edge load and loss up to 2.1 pct, even though throughput is already low.
